Some harnesses attach optional MCP servers lazily: if an initial tool-catalog scan does not show T3 tools, do not conclude that cross-provider delegation is unavailable. Make one bounded direct attempt using the known T3 tool name on the next tool step. In Codex code mode, for example, call `tools.mcp__t3_code__orchestrator_capabilities({})` before reporting that the capability is absent. Keep polling/wait loops bounded, do not duplicate active work, and use stable `clientRequestId` values when retrying tools that accept them.

ACP fallback: some ACP agents accept the injected MCP server but fail to expose its tools. When the T3 tools are absent and `T3_ACP_MCP_NODE` is present, call the same tools through the terminal: `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 "$T3_ACP_MCP_NODE" ${T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT:+"$T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT"} acp-mcp-call orchestrator_capabilities '{}'` (`T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT` is unset when T3 runs as a standalone executable). Delegate with `acp-mcp-call delegate_task '{"task":"...","target":{"providerInstanceId":"...","model":"..."},"mode":"async","clientRequestId":"..."}'`. This is the supported T3 transport fallback, not an ordinary shell-based substitute for delegation.

### Showing visuals

When a chart, table, diagram, image collage, or mockup would say more than prose, build a self-contained HTML page, check it with `html_preview`, then publish it with `html_render` before your final reply. The reader sees the page above that reply, so don't announce or restate it; add only what it doesn't say.

- When model options are requested or the child keeps the parent's provider instance and model with nonempty `inheritedOptions` from `orchestrator_capabilities`, use `delegate_task` even for native-supported models. Native subagents cannot reliably apply T3 model options. Read the selected model's descriptors from `orchestrator_capabilities` and put settings in `target.options`, not only in the prompt. Claude commonly uses {"effort":"max","fastMode":true}; Codex uses {"reasoningEffort":"max","serviceTier":"priority"}. Do not translate max to high or ignore unsupported settings: report a capability mismatch. Options inherit only for the same provider instance and model; explicit entries override individual values, and [] or {} clears them. Check the returned providerInstanceId, model, and options against the requested selection.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

channel.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

q.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendMessage
tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

tools.name: ShareOnboardingGuide
tools.description:
Upload the ONBOARDING.md in the current directory and return a share link teammates can open in Claude Code. Call this after the user has confirmed the final content.

When called with the default mode='check': if a local ONBOARDING.md is present, uploads it to the most-recently-updated org guide (or creates one if none exist) and returns a fresh link. If no local file is present, returns the existing link without uploading (status: has_existing).

mode.description: 'check' (default): if ONBOARDING.md is present locally, uploads it to the most-recent guide (creates one if none exist); otherwise reports the existing link without uploading. 'update': upload to a specific guide by short_code. 'create': always make a new link. 'delete': remove a guide.

short_code.description: Short code of a specific guide to target (returned by a previous call). Honored by check, update, and delete — skips the org-wide lookup and targets this guide directly.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

args.description: Optional arguments for the skill

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

tools.name: WebSearch
tools.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

Task 3 review: one latent defect to fix, and three tests to add. Commit them forward as a new commit; do not amend.

**Defect:** `unclaim` (about `registry.py:173-174`) and `release` (about `:201-202`) forget *every* key in the slot through `_keys`. That includes a key still being cleared after another entry gave the slot up. Reproduction:
1. Entry `a` holds `(3,"pin")` and `(3,"password")`, then calls `give_up(3)`.
2. Before the clears run, entry `b` claims `(3,"pin")` only, with `want`.
3. `b` calls `unclaim(3)`, or `release`.

Both keys are forgotten, so the password stays on the lock. That's a give-up the user asked for, silently dropped. With integer keys it can't happen, because an owned slot's key is never `release=True`.

**Fix:** in those two forget paths only, skip keys still being cleared, for example:

```python
for key in self._keys(entry, slot):
    if not entry.worker.slots[key].release:
        entry.worker.forget(key)
```

A comprehension or a filtered `_keys` is fine, whichever reads best. Add one short comment saying why: a clear another entry gave up goes on without an owner. Leave `give_up` as it is.

**Tests to add** to `tests/sync/test_registry.py`. Each one must kill the named mutant: run each mutation, see the test fail, and restore the file.
1. The scenario above, through `unclaim`. Assert that the password clear still reaches the lock (`(3,"password")` is gone from `lock.codes` after settling) and that `b`'s PIN key is forgotten. The mutant is removing your new filter.
2. `release` with a two-key slot: `release("front","a")` leaves `worker.slots` without slot 3's keys and leaves `lock.codes` unchanged. The mutant is `release` forgetting only the first key.
3. `hold` refuses another entry claiming a different key in an owned slot: `pytest.raises(SlotTaken)` around `registry.hold("front","b",{(3,"password"):"x"})` while `a` owns slot 3. The mutant is `_hold` checking the raw key instead of `slot_of(key)`.
4. `write_once("front",(3,"password"),"x")` raises `SlotTaken` while `a` owns slot 3. The mutant is `write_once` checking the raw key.

Then run `tests/sync` and `tests/test_architecture.py`, and commit with `--no-verify`, for the same mypy reason as before. Report as before, including each mutant and the test that killed it.

content.thinking:
I'm noticing that the UTF-16BE conversion function will crash on an odd-length byte array, since reading a 16-bit value at the last byte goes out of bounds and throws a RangeError.

Comparing how different CCs handle this: NodeNaming explicitly validates even length and treats odd-length payloads as invalid, dropping the CC entirely. But User Credential CC's User Report and User Notification don't have this check, so an odd-length string there would throw rather than be caught as a validation failure — that's inconsistent.

For passwords specifically, falling back to raw bytes on odd length seems more lenient. I'm weighing whether to apply the strict validatePayload approach everywhere like NodeNaming does, but that risks dropping an entire Credential Report (and losing slot occupancy info) just because a lock firmware stored a malformed password using UTF-8 instead of UTF-16 — which seems too harsh given some vendor implementations may not follow the UTF-16 convention we expect.

content.thinking: I think I have enough to respond with my findings and recommendation, letting Raman decide himself per policy, and offering to make the change once he confirms. My recommendation is to standardize on the shared validatePayload helper for consistency, applying it to both the username decoders and the password handling rather than mixing approaches.

content.text:
AlCalzone, the zwave-js maintainer, left one comment on `UserCredentialCC.ts:89`. Copilot found no issues.

> "There are a few other locations where UTF-16 strings are sent. Lets make sure we handle them consistently in terms of what we do with uneven lengths."

He's right: there are four places that decode UTF-16, and each handles an odd byte count differently.

| Where | What happens on an odd length |
|---|---|
| Node Naming CC, `decodeNodeTextPayload` (`NodeNamingCC.ts:84`) | `validatePayload(textBuffer.length % 2 === 0)`: a clean "invalid payload" error |
| User Credential CC user name, User Report (`UserCredentialCC.ts:2065`) | No check. The shared decoder throws a bare `RangeError: Offset is outside the bounds of the DataView` (I reproduced this against the built package) |
| User Credential CC user name, User Notification report (`:2271`) | The same bare `RangeError` |
| Our password decode (`:88`) | Returns the raw bytes |

So two of the user-name sites predate our PR and have the bug, and our raw-bytes fallback is a third behavior.

I recommend `validatePayload` everywhere. Node Naming already does it, the spec makes odd-length UTF-16 a malformed frame, and it turns the two `RangeError` crashes into proper invalid-payload errors. That means adding the even-length check to both user-name decoders and switching the password path from raw bytes to `validatePayload`. The cost is that a Credential Report carrying an odd-length password would be rejected whole, instead of passing through as raw bytes. The only way that happens is a lock storing non-UTF-16 bytes, for example one programmed through a vendor app that sends UTF-8. That's the one judgment call here.

The alternative is to keep the raw bytes for passwords, on the grounds that credential data is opaque bytes for every other type, and add `validatePayload` only to the two user names. It's defensible, but it's not the consistency he asked for.

Under zwave-js's AI policy, the reply on the PR should be yours. Tell me which way you want it, and I'll make the change in `~/projects/node-zwave-js-u3c-password`, with tests for each decode site, for you to review before anything is pushed.

The Task 8 review for the LCM work is still running in the background.

When the LCM sync worker was re-keyed from int slots to `CredentialAddress` (password PR 1, 2026-10-23), every place that still passed an int did nothing instead of failing. `x in worker.slots`, `.get()`, `request_sync`, `forget` and `resume` all silently miss. mypy did not catch the membership tests.

What the reviews found:
- five negative assertions (`2 not in worker.slots`) that now passed whatever happened;
- two more in the zha tests;
- a shared conftest helper (`async_trigger_sync_tick`) that had stopped requesting any sync, which about 14 tests depend on.

A green suite showed none of these.

A second finding: a generic registry's "forget every key in the slot" also forgot a key another entry had given up and that was still being cleared. That can't happen with one key per slot. With several keys, a removed user's password would have stayed on the lock.

**How to apply:** after any re-key, grep for every membership test, lookup and helper that takes the key, and judge each one. Have the reviewer hunt for silent no-ops explicitly, not only failures. When one key per unit becomes many, re-check every "act on all keys in the unit" path against keys owned by someone else or in flight. Related: [[feedback_a_shim_can_hide_the_defect_it_shims]], [[feedback_mutation_must_reach_the_invariant]].
EOF

9. **Fingerprints for types no longer tracked are kept.** `remember` keeps the last fingerprint of a type the worker stops tracking, for example after a lock loses password support. If that type comes back, recall trusts the stale write. Confirm that's wanted.

- Worker debug logs name a credential type with its slot ("slot 3 pin").
- Every existing test passes unchanged apart from how keys and the store/diagnostics shapes are spelled. The `tests/sync` suite only gained tests, for keys that hold a slot and a type.

## Assessment
**Ready to open** once the `CredentialAddress` docstring is fixed. The Minor items are cheap and worth folding in, but none blocks.</result>

# Password PR 2: what PR 1 left for it

Gathered from the final whole-branch review of PR 1 (branch `feat/credential-address-core`, 2026-10-23). Every item is fine while every address is a PIN, and each must be decided when PASSWORD addresses appear. Paths and lines are as of PR 1's head.

1. **One release per slot.** `give_up` sends a release clear for every tracked key in the slot. `port.releasing` and `_written` are per slot, so the first clear deletes the user and each later key sends a second release. Make the later release idempotent: return `False` and let the read-back find the slot empty. Don't make the worker look inside keys.
2. **`release(written=…)` reads only the PIN.** `LockStore.wrote_pin` (`ha/lock_store.py`) feeds it. A slot holding only a password needs "Lock Code Manager wrote any type here".
3. **Repair issue ids are per slot** (`ha/runtime.py` `async_reconcile_issues`). With two addresses in a slot, one in sync can delete a `slot_suspended_*` / `slot_disabled_*` issue that a held one just raised, depending on dict order. Aggregate per slot before raising or deleting.
4. **`_on_disable(address)` turns the whole slot off.** Decide what a refused password does when the PIN is fine (spec decision 4: a slot needs at least one credential).
5. **The in-sync entities read only the PIN.** `LockWorkerView._pin` (`entity.py`) drives both the aggregate `in_sync` and `pin_in_sync`. The binary sensor already stores `self._addresses`, which nothing uses: aggregate over them.
6. **The adapter routes by PIN only.**
   - `_pin_slot` refuses a whole read batch if any address isn't a PIN.
   - `pushed`, `others`, `_writing`, `_written_at` and `wants_pin` are keyed by slot number and are PIN-only.
   - `_Coordinator.observe_push` and `desired_credential` drop the type.
   - Echo suppression is per slot, so a password write would swallow a PIN push for the same slot.
7. **The HA-layer entry points are PIN-only.** `async_hold_lock(wants: Mapping[int, Want])`, `async_want`, `async_write_once` and `async_resume_slot` (which calls `write_once(pin_address(slot))`) need the per-lock managed address set.
8. **Occupancy reads only PINs.** `_async_occupied` (`ha/allocation.py`) needs every managed type the lock takes: a slot holding only a password is occupied.
9. **Fingerprints for types no longer tracked are kept.** `remember` keeps the last fingerprint of a type the worker stops tracking, for example after a lock loses password support. If that type comes back, recall trusts the stale write. Confirm that's wanted, or drop such fingerprints when a type leaves the lock's capabilities.
10. **Already right for PR 2:** `_duplicate_of` filters to PIN (duplicates are per type), and `lock_codes` shows only PINs (it is the lock card's PIN view).

Also from earlier PR 1 reviews:
- The test helper `async_trigger_sync_tick` (`tests/conftest.py`) is correct now, but no test depends on it, because the worker already syncs on `want`. Either drop its `request_sync`, or make one test depend on it.
- Downgrade after PR 1: an older release can't read the version 2 store, so setup fails. Recovery is a backup restore, or deleting `.storage/lock_code_manager.core`. Deleting it costs one rewrite of each PIN on locks that hide their codes, and forgets any clears still owed.

# Password PR 2: what PR 1 left for it

Gathered from the final whole-branch review of PR 1 (branch `feat/credential-address-core`, 2026-10-23). Every item is fine while every address is a PIN, and each must be decided when PASSWORD addresses appear. Paths and lines are as of PR 1's head.

1. **One release per slot.** `give_up` sends a release clear for every tracked key in the slot. `port.releasing` and `_written` are per slot, so the first clear deletes the user and each later key sends a second release. Make the later release idempotent: return `False` and let the read-back find the slot empty. Don't make the worker look inside keys.
2. **`release(written=…)` reads only the PIN.** `LockStore.wrote_pin` (`ha/lock_store.py`) feeds it. A slot holding only a password needs "Lock Code Manager wrote any type here".
3. **Repair issue ids are per slot** (`ha/runtime.py` `async_reconcile_issues`). With two addresses in a slot, one in sync can delete a `slot_suspended_*` / `slot_disabled_*` issue that a held one just raised, depending on dict order. Aggregate per slot before raising or deleting.
4. **`_on_disable(address)` turns the whole slot off.** Decide what a refused password does when the PIN is fine (spec decision 4: a slot needs at least one credential).
5. **The in-sync entities read only the PIN.** `LockWorkerView._pin` (`entity.py`) drives both the aggregate `in_sync` and `pin_in_sync`. The binary sensor already stores `self._addresses`, which nothing uses: aggregate over them.
6. **The adapter routes by PIN only.**
   - `_pin_slot` refuses a whole read batch if any address isn't a PIN.
   - `pushed`, `others`, `_writing`, `_written_at` and `wants_pin` are keyed by slot number and are PIN-only.
   - `_Coordinator.observe_push` and `desired_credential` drop the type.
   - Echo suppression is per slot, so a password write would swallow a PIN push for the same slot.
7. **The HA-layer entry points are PIN-only.** `async_hold_lock(wants: Mapping[int, Want])`, `async_want`, `async_write_once` and `async_resume_slot` (which calls `write_once(pin_address(slot))`) need the per-lock managed address set.
8. **Occupancy reads only PINs.** `_async_occupied` (`ha/allocation.py`) needs every managed type the lock takes: a slot holding only a password is occupied.
9. **Fingerprints for types no longer tracked are kept.** `remember` keeps the last fingerprint of a type the worker stops tracking, for example after a lock loses password support. If that type comes back, recall trusts the stale write. Confirm that's wanted, or drop such fingerprints when a type leaves the lock's capabilities.
10. **Already right for PR 2:** `_duplicate_of` filters to PIN (duplicates are per type), and `lock_codes` shows only PINs (it is the lock card's PIN view).

Also from earlier PR 1 reviews:
- The test helper `async_trigger_sync_tick` (`tests/conftest.py`) is correct now, but no test depends on it, because the worker already syncs on `want`. Either drop its `request_sync`, or make one test depend on it.
- Downgrade after PR 1: an older release can't read the version 2 store, so setup fails. Recovery is a backup restore, or deleting `.storage/lock_code_manager.core`. Deleting it costs one rewrite of each PIN on locks that hide their codes, and forgets any clears still owed.

content.text:
The final whole-branch review found nothing critical. It says PR 1 can be opened once one item is fixed: the `CredentialAddress` docstring still says `user_ref` will one day become the user's name. This PR makes the slot number the thing everything keys on, so the docstring needs rewording.

The review also turned up three small unintended behavior changes:
- When several slots are already taken by another entry, the warnings could now come out in a different order.
- Rebuilding a re-paired lock now drops more of the worker's state than it did before.
- Batched debug log lines now read `(1 pin, 2 pin)` instead of `(1, 2)`. I'm keeping that one, since the type is the point.

A subagent is now applying the docstring fix and the cheap minor items:
- restore the original order for the "slot taken" warnings;
- make the re-pair rebuild forget only the slots being cleared, as before;
- add a comment on the registry's one easy-to-miss default;
- a few renames so "slot" consistently means a slot number;
- two readability tweaks in `ha/runtime.py`;
- one store test switched from a hand-built fake worker to a real one.

I saved the reviewer's list of nine things PR 2 has to handle to `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-23-password-pr2-carryover.md`. The biggest ones:
- **One release per slot:** releasing a slot currently sends a separate clear for every credential type in it.
- **Repair issues collide per slot:** two credential types in one slot can raise and delete each other's repair issue.
- **Refused password:** decide what happens when the lock refuses a password but the PIN is fine.
- **Sync sensors are PIN-only:** the in-sync sensors look only at the PIN.

**Downgrades:** once a user upgrades, an older release can't read the new store, and Lock Code Manager won't set up at all. Recovery is to restore a backup, or delete `.storage/lock_code_manager.core`. Deleting it means each PIN is written once more on locks that hide their codes, and any pending clears are forgotten. I'll put that in the PR body.

Once the fixes pass, I'll ask you before pushing and opening the PR.

The zwave-js#9396 question is still open: should an odd-length UTF-16 string be rejected as an invalid payload everywhere, passwords included? I recommend yes.

input.content:
## Proposed change

The first of four PRs toward password credentials. It re-keys the sync engine from a bare slot number to a credential address, `(slot, credential type)`, and changes no behavior: every address is a PIN for now.

- The sync engine (`sync/`: worker, port and registry) is now generic over its key, because `sync/` may not import `model/`. The integration keys it by `CredentialAddress`. The worker never looks inside a key.
- An entry still owns a whole slot. The registry is told which slot a key is in (`slot_of`), so claiming, giving up and letting go of a slot act on every credential type in it. Letting go never drops a clear another entry gave up and that is still being sent.
- The provider adapter turns an address back into today's slot-based provider calls. Any other credential type is refused before anything reaches the lock.
- The lock store moves to version 2 and keeps what was last written per credential type: `{"wrote": {"pin": …}}`. Version 1 records are migrated on load. The fingerprint itself is unchanged, so no lock is written again after the upgrade.
- Diagnostics nest each lock's worker slots by credential type: `slots["3"]["pin"]`.
- Worker debug logs name the credential type with the slot: `slot 3 pin`.

**Downgrading:** once upgraded, an earlier release cannot read the version 2 store (Home Assistant refuses a newer store version), and Lock Code Manager won't set up. To go back, restore a backup, or delete `.storage/lock_code_manager.core`. Deleting it means each PIN is written again on locks that hide their codes, and any clears still owed are forgotten. This doesn't affect upgrading, so there is no Breaking change section.

**Testing:**
- `tests/sync/` gained tests for keys that hold a slot and a type, and no existing line in it changed, so it serves as the oracle for the re-key.
- Elsewhere, every test passes, changed only in how keys and the store and diagnostics shapes are spelled.
- Full suite: 3373 passed. Coverage is equal to `main`, with no line newly uncovered. Property tests pass at the CI profile.
- Mutation checks covered the multi-key registry paths and the store migration.

PR 1 is finished on `feat/credential-address-core`, but nothing has been pushed. I'm waiting for your go-ahead.

**What the branch does:** the sync engine is now keyed by slot and credential type instead of a bare slot number, and the lock store moves to version 2. Every key is still a PIN, so behavior should not change. The existing engine tests (`tests/sync/`) only gained tests and have no edited lines, which is the main evidence for that.

**Verification:**
- The full suite passes: 3373 tests.
- Coverage is 99.38%, against 99.37% on `main`. Both runs miss the same lines, so the branch leaves nothing newly uncovered.
- Property tests and mypy pass.
- Every task was reviewed, and the whole branch had a final review.

**What the reviews caught and fixed:**
- **A latent ownership bug:** with several credentials per slot, one entry letting go of a slot could drop another entry's pending clear. That would have left a removed user's password working on the lock. It was fixed with tests.
- **Silent no-op tests:** after the re-key, any leftover integer key just misses instead of raising an error. That left seven assertions checking nothing and one shared test helper doing nothing. All are fixed, and a reviewer recorded every key reaching the engine across the whole suite and found none left over.

**Three changes users can notice:**
- **Diagnostics:** each lock's slots are now nested by credential type, as `slots["3"]["pin"]`.
- **Debug logs:** worker lines now say `slot 3 pin` instead of `slot 3`.
- **Downgrades:** after upgrading, an older release can't read the new store and Lock Code Manager won't set up. Recovery is restoring a backup, or deleting `.storage/lock_code_manager.core`. Deleting it means each PIN is written once more on locks that hide their codes, and any pending clears are forgotten. The PR body says this, outside a Breaking Change section, because upgrading is unaffected.

The PR body follows the template and is drafted at `/tmp/lcm-pr1/pr-body.md`. The type is "Code quality improvements". The reviewers' list of what PR 2 has to handle is saved at `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-23-password-pr2-carryover.md`.

**Shall I push `feat/credential-address-core` and open the PR against `main`?**

Separately, on zwave-js#9396 I still need your call on odd-length UTF-16. I recommend rejecting it as an invalid payload at every decode site, passwords included.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

The zwave-js change is committed locally as `eb51d7843` on `fix/u3c-password-utf16`, but not pushed. It now rejects odd-length UTF-16 as an invalid payload everywhere, passwords included. It's ready for your review, and under the zwave-js AI policy the reply to AlCalzone is yours to write.

**What changed in `UserCredentialCC.ts`:**
- **User names:** the User Set and User Report parsers now check for an even length, the same `validatePayload(length % 2 === 0)` that Node Naming CC already uses.
- **Passwords:** the Credential Set parser and the Credential Report parser check for an even length. The Credential Report only checks when the lock actually sent the password back.
- **`normalizeCredentialData`:** passwords always go through the UTF-16 decoder now, since an odd length can no longer get that far. The raw-bytes fallback is gone.

**Facts for your reply:**
- A malformed command doesn't throw. `CommandClass.parse` turns an invalid payload into an `InvalidCC`, which is logged as INVALID and dropped, the same as any other malformed command.
- Before this change, an odd-length UTF-16 user name made the decoder throw a bare `RangeError`. That isn't a Z-Wave error, so it escaped `CommandClass.parse` uncaught. The PR fixes that bug too, not just the password case.

**Tests:**
- New file `packages/zwave-js/src/lib/test/cc/UserCredentialCC.test.ts` with nine tests. Each parse site has an odd-length case that must come back as `InvalidCC`, and an even-length case that must decode correctly. There is also one case pinning that a Credential Report without the password sent back isn't length-checked.
- I dropped the raw-bytes unit test.
- The five User Credential test files all pass: 67 tests.
- Removing each of the four checks fails exactly its own test.
- oxlint and the formatter pass.
- tsc reports 110 errors in the zwave-js package and 2 in the command class package, none in the files this commit touches. I didn't confirm they also occur on the base commit.

To review: `git -C ~/projects/node-zwave-js-u3c-password show eb51d7843`.

content.text:
I don't think it's a GitHub error. GitHub's status page shows everything operational, and the evidence points to something on your Mac:

- **The block is per program.** From the same shell, `nc` and both `curl`s connect to `github.com:443` in about 10 ms. git's HTTPS helper (`git-remote-https`) and `gh` hang at the TCP connect step, before any HTTP is sent. It happens with every GitHub address, including ones `curl` reached seconds earlier.
- **Little Snitch is active.** Its network extension is running, and Little Snitch can allow or deny connections per program.
- **git was replaced today.** Homebrew installed a new git (2.56.0_1) at 14:14, so `git-remote-https` is a new binary in a new Cellar path. An existing allow rule may not cover it, which would leave the connection denied or waiting on a prompt. That fits your terminal hanging too.

I can't confirm the `gh` side: its binary is from October 21, so a rule for it may have expired or be waiting on a prompt for some other reason.

What to check in Little Snitch:
1. Look for a pending prompt, or a deny rule, for `git-remote-https` (under `/opt/homebrew/Cellar/git/2.56.0_1/…`) and for `gh`.
2. Allow both to connect to `github.com` and `api.github.com`.

Tell me once that's done, and I'll push both branches and open the LCM PR. If you'd rather do it yourself, the commands from my last message still apply.

## Proposed change

The first of four PRs toward password credentials. It re-keys the sync engine from a bare slot number to a credential address, `(slot, credential type)`, and changes no behavior: every address is a PIN for now.

- The sync engine (`sync/`: worker, port and registry) is now generic over its key, because `sync/` may not import `model/`. The integration keys it by `CredentialAddress`. The worker never looks inside a key.
- An entry still owns a whole slot. The registry is told which slot a key is in (`slot_of`), so claiming, giving up and letting go of a slot act on every credential type in it. Letting go never drops a clear another entry gave up and that is still being sent.
- The provider adapter turns an address back into today's slot-based provider calls. Any other credential type is refused before anything reaches the lock.
- The lock store moves to version 2 and keeps what was last written per credential type: `{"wrote": {"pin": …}}`. Version 1 records are migrated on load. The fingerprint itself is unchanged, so no lock is written again after the upgrade.
- Diagnostics nest each lock's worker slots by credential type: `slots["3"]["pin"]`.
- Worker debug logs name the credential type with the slot: `slot 3 pin`.

**Downgrading:** once upgraded, an earlier release cannot read the version 2 store (Home Assistant refuses a newer store version), and Lock Code Manager won't set up. To go back, restore a backup, or delete `.storage/lock_code_manager.core`. Deleting it means each PIN is written again on locks that hide their codes, and any clears still owed are forgotten. This doesn't affect upgrading, so there is no Breaking change section.

**Testing:**
- `tests/sync/` gained tests for keys that hold a slot and a type, and no existing line in it changed, so it serves as the oracle for the re-key.
- Elsewhere, every test passes, changed only in how keys and the store and diagnostics shapes are spelled.
- Full suite: 3373 passed. Coverage is equal to `main`, with no line newly uncovered. Property tests pass at the CI profile.
- Mutation checks covered the multi-key registry paths and the store migration.

## Type of change

- [ ] Dependency upgrade
- [ ] Bugfix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)
- [ ] New feature (which adds functionality)
- [ ] Breaking change (fix/feature causing existing functionality to break)
- [x] Code quality improvements to existing code or addition of tests

## Additional information

- This PR fixes or closes issue: none
- This PR is related to issue: password credential support, PR 1 of 4: core re-key → password in the model and HA layer → cards → Z-Wave, which needs zwave-js/zwave-js#9396 first

# Password PR 2: what PR 1 left for it

Gathered from the final whole-branch review of PR 1 (branch `feat/credential-address-core`, 2026-10-23). Every item is fine while every address is a PIN, and each must be decided when PASSWORD addresses appear. Paths and lines are as of PR 1's head.

1. **One release per slot.** `give_up` sends a release clear for every tracked key in the slot. `port.releasing` and `_written` are per slot, so the first clear deletes the user and each later key sends a second release. Make the later release idempotent: return `False` and let the read-back find the slot empty. Don't make the worker look inside keys.
2. **`release(written=…)` reads only the PIN.** `LockStore.wrote_pin` (`ha/lock_store.py`) feeds it. A slot holding only a password needs "Lock Code Manager wrote any type here".
3. **Repair issue ids are per slot** (`ha/runtime.py` `async_reconcile_issues`). With two addresses in a slot, one in sync can delete a `slot_suspended_*` / `slot_disabled_*` issue that a held one just raised, depending on dict order. Aggregate per slot before raising or deleting.
4. **`_on_disable(address)` turns the whole slot off.** Decide what a refused password does when the PIN is fine (spec decision 4: a slot needs at least one credential).
5. **The in-sync entities read only the PIN.** `LockWorkerView._pin` (`entity.py`) drives both the aggregate `in_sync` and `pin_in_sync`. The binary sensor already stores `self._addresses`, which nothing uses: aggregate over them.
6. **The adapter routes by PIN only.**
   - `_pin_slot` refuses a whole read batch if any address isn't a PIN.
   - `pushed`, `others`, `_writing`, `_written_at` and `wants_pin` are keyed by slot number and are PIN-only.
   - `_Coordinator.observe_push` and `desired_credential` drop the type.
   - Echo suppression is per slot, so a password write would swallow a PIN push for the same slot.
7. **The HA-layer entry points are PIN-only.** `async_hold_lock(wants: Mapping[int, Want])`, `async_want`, `async_write_once` and `async_resume_slot` (which calls `write_once(pin_address(slot))`) need the per-lock managed address set.
8. **Occupancy reads only PINs.** `_async_occupied` (`ha/allocation.py`) needs every managed type the lock takes: a slot holding only a password is occupied.
9. **Fingerprints for types no longer tracked are kept.** `remember` keeps the last fingerprint of a type the worker stops tracking, for example after a lock loses password support. If that type comes back, recall trusts the stale write. Confirm that's wanted, or drop such fingerprints when a type leaves the lock's capabilities.
10. **Already right for PR 2:** `_duplicate_of` filters to PIN (duplicates are per type), and `lock_codes` shows only PINs (it is the lock card's PIN view).

Also from earlier PR 1 reviews:
- The test helper `async_trigger_sync_tick` (`tests/conftest.py`) is correct now, but no test depends on it, because the worker already syncs on `want`. Either drop its `request_sync`, or make one test depend on it.
- Downgrade after PR 1: an older release can't read the version 2 store, so setup fails. Recovery is a backup restore, or deleting `.storage/lock_code_manager.core`. Deleting it costs one rewrite of each PIN on locks that hide their codes, and forgets any clears still owed.

# Reviewing one task of PR 1

Context first: read `/tmp/lcm-pr1/context.md` (the shared context and rules the implementer worked under) and `/tmp/lcm-pr1/head.md` (the plan header). The task's requirements are in `/tmp/lcm-pr1/task<N>.md`. The code is in the worktree `/Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/.worktrees/credential-address-core`. Inspect the task's commits with `git -C <worktree> diff <BASE> <HEAD>`, and read the changed files in full where needed.

You are read-only. Do not edit, commit or stash anything. Running tests and `prek run mypy --all-files` from the worktree is fine.

## Stage 1: spec compliance

Do not trust the implementer's report. Read the code and compare it with the task text line by line.
- **Missing:** anything the task asked for that isn't there, or is claimed but not done.
- **Extra:** anything built that the task didn't ask for, over-engineering, or unrelated edits.
- **Misread:** the right feature built the wrong way, or a different reading of the requirement.
- **PR 1 is a no-behavior-change refactor.** Flag any changed test **expected value** outside what the task names (key spellings, the store's nested `wrote`, the diagnostics nesting).
- Where the implementer deviated from the task text because the code differed, judge whether they kept the task's intent.

If Stage 1 finds issues, report them and **stop**: no Stage 2.

## Stage 2: code quality (only if Stage 1 is clean)

- **Correctness:** edge cases, and anything mypy can't see.
- **Test quality:** do the new tests reach the invariant they name? Would the mutation the task describes kill them? You may run the mutation yourself, but restore the file in a `finally`-style way, confirm `git -C <worktree> status` is clean afterwards, and say that you did.
- **Fit with the code around it:** comment density and voice (terse, intent not history, no `Args:`/`Returns:`), naming, idiom (comprehensions, no inline imports, no `nonlocal`, `@override`), and the layer import rules.
- **Leaks:** no credential value in any log or error message.
- Don't flag pre-existing issues the task didn't touch.

## Report

```
Stage 1: ✅ compliant | ❌ issues
  - file:line: what is missing, extra or misread
Stage 2: (only if Stage 1 ✅)
  Strengths: …
  Issues: Critical / Important / Minor, each with file:line and a concrete fix
  Assessment: APPROVED | CHANGES REQUESTED
```

- computer-use: OS/window-level inspection and input in visible local app windows through `orca computer`: native apps, external browser windows (Chrome, Edge, Safari), and app webviews. Not for Orca's embedded browser (use `orca-cli`) or page-only automation (use Playwright or CDP).
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- mempalace: MemPalace is the user's central, persistent memory system — hosted on docker-server and accessed via mcphub MCP aggregation. Use when asked about mempalace, the memory palace, recalling past work / decisions / preferences, saving learnings, the user's projects / homelab / family / career, or wing/room/drawer organization. Also use proactively whenever the conversation touches user-specific facts that may already exist in the palace.
- orca-cli: Operate Orca-managed worktrees, folder contexts, terminals, repos, automations, artifacts, skill sharing, worktree comments, and Orca's embedded browser through the `orca` CLI. Use when the user says "$orca-cli", "Orca worktree", "child worktree", "spawn codex/claude in a worktree", "read/wait/send Orca terminal", "handoff" / "handover" / "give this to another agent", "Orca browser", "orca artifacts", or "share skills". Prefer it over raw git worktree, ad hoc PTYs, or Computer Use when Orca state is involved. Use Computer Use only for external windows or desktop UI that needs OS-level control, and Playwright or CDP for external pages.
- orchestration: Coordinate supervised Orca workers: threaded messages, blocking ask/reply, task dispatch, worker_done/escalation waits, task DAGs, decision gates, coordinator loops, and decomposing work across agents. Use `orca-cli` for full ownership handoffs — "hand off", "handoff", "handover", "give this to another agent", "another worktree" — unless asked to supervise, monitor, or coordinate a DAG, and for terminal control, lightweight terminal prompts, shell commands, Orca worktree management, and reading or waiting on terminals. Use Computer Use for external browser windows, webviews, Orca app UI, or desktop UI outside Orca's embedded browser only when the task requires OS/window-level control such as focus, menus, dialogs, coordinates, or screenshots. Use `orca-cli` for Orca's embedded pages and a page-automation tool such as Playwright or CDP for external pages.
