tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. """
What the lock workers remember across a restart, in one Home Assistant Store.

Per lock, keyed by the entity registry id its worker is bound to, so a rename
keeps it (#1442) and a device re-paired under the same entity id never finds
the old one's, with its entity id beside it: whether the lock has ever
answered, whether a read of it has ever described a slot (#1581; absent in a
record saved before, and then not known to), and per slot what was last
written -- a keyed fingerprint or ``cleared``, never a PIN -- and a release
clear still owed, with the entry that gave the slot up. What a slot holds is
read again; counts, fights and holds start over (a hold's repair outlives a
restart on its own).

Written a second after a change, and at Home Assistant's final write. Never
dropped on an unload (#1243): only when a release is done, a slot is let go
of for good, a lock leaves Lock Code Manager or an entry is deleted. A
record whose registry id is gone goes at the next start.
"""

from collections.abc import Callable, Collection
from typing import Any

from homeassistant.core import HomeAssistant, callback
from homeassistant.helpers import entity_registry as er
from homeassistant.helpers.storage import Store

from ..const import DOMAIN
from ..sync.slot import CLEARED
from ..sync.worker import LockWorker

STORE_KEY = f"{DOMAIN}.core"
STORE_VERSION = 1
SAVE_DELAY = 1.0

Record = dict[str, Any]


class LockStore:
    """Each lock's record, under ``key``: the registry id its worker is bound to."""

    def __init__(self, hass: HomeAssistant) -> None:
        """Start empty; ``async_load`` reads what was saved."""
        self._hass = hass
        self._store: Store[dict[str, Any]] = Store(hass, STORE_VERSION, STORE_KEY)
        self._locks: dict[str, Record] = {}

    async def async_load(self) -> None:
        """Read what was saved, each record under its lock's current entity id."""
        saved = await self._store.async_load() or {}
        self._locks = saved.get("locks", {})
        registry = er.async_get(self._hass)
        for key, record in self._locks.items():
            if (entity := registry.async_get(key)) is not None:
                record["entity_id"] = entity.entity_id

    # What a lock's worker starts from ------------------------------------------

    def wrote(self, key: str, slot: int) -> str | None:
        """Return what was last written to ``slot`` on the lock, if anything."""
        record = self._locks.get(key)
        return (
            None if record is None else record["slots"].get(str(slot), {}).get("wrote")
        )

    def wrote_pin(self, key: str, slot: int) -> bool:
        """
        Return whether a PIN was what was last written to ``slot`` on the lock.

        A slot only ever cleared never held Lock Code Manager's code.
        """
        return self.wrote(key, slot) not in (None, CLEARED)

    def answered(self, key: str) -> bool:
        """Return whether the lock has ever answered."""
        record = self._locks.get(key)
        return record is not None and record["answered"]

    def reports(self, key: str) -> bool:
        """Return whether a read of the lock has ever described a slot."""
        record = self._locks.get(key)
        return record is not None and record.get("reports", False)

    def releases(self) -> list[tuple[str, int, str]]:
        """Return each release clear still owed: lock, slot, the entry that gave it up."""
        return [
            (record["entity_id"], int(slot), saved["release"])
            for record in self._locks.values()
            for slot, saved in record["slots"].items()
            if "release" in saved
        ]

    # Keeping it current --------------------------------------------------------

    @callback
    def remember(
        self,
        key: str,
        lock: str,
        worker: LockWorker,
        given_up_by: Callable[[int], str | None],
    ) -> None:
        """
        Take what ``worker`` knows of ``lock`` now; slots it no longer tracks keep theirs.

        A release is kept while it is still going, not once held: its repair
        brings it back. ``given_up_by`` names the entry that gave a slot up.
        """
        record = self._locks.get(key, {"answered": False, "slots": {}})
        slots = dict(record["slots"])
        for number, slot in worker.slots.items():
            saved: dict[str, str] = {}
            if slot.wrote is not None:
                saved["wrote"] = slot.wrote
            if slot.release and slot.hold is None and (by := given_up_by(number)):
                saved["release"] = by
            if saved:
                slots[str(number)] = saved
            else:
                slots.pop(str(number), None)
        self._put(
            key,
            {
                **record,
                "entity_id": lock,
                "answered": worker.answered_ever,
                "slots": slots,
            },
        )

    @callback
    def reported(self, key: str, lock: str) -> None:
        """Remember that a read of ``lock`` has described a slot."""
        record = self._locks.get(key, {"answered": False, "slots": {}})
        self._put(key, {**record, "entity_id": lock, "reports": True})

    @callback
    def unreported(self, key: str) -> None:
        """Forget that a read of the lock has described a slot: it is asked again."""
        if (record := self._locks.get(key)) is not None:
            self._put(key, {k: v for k, v in record.items() if k != "reports"})

    @callback
    def forget_slot(self, key: str, slot: int) -> None:
        """Forget ``slot`` on the lock: it is done, or let go of for good."""
        if (record := self._locks.get(key)) is not None:
            slots = {n: s for n, s in record["slots"].items() if n != str(slot)}
            self._put(key, {**record, "slots": slots})

    @callback
    def forget_lock(self, key: str) -> None:

The user has a point — the v2 bump happened because `wrote` changed from a string to a dict, not just because a key was added. content.text:
You're right, the version bump isn't necessary. It came from a choice I made, not from anything Home Assistant requires.

**Why it happened:** I didn't add a key, I changed the type of an existing one. `wrote` used to be a string (the PIN's fingerprint, or `cleared`); in PR 1 it became a dict, `{"pin": …}`. Changing the type of a key that code already reads is what needed a migration. A migration in Home Assistant's `Store` means raising the major version, and the downgrade problem follows from that. I checked `homeassistant/helpers/storage.py`: on load, Home Assistant raises `UnsupportedStorageVersionError` only when the stored major version is newer than what the code can read. That is exactly what we'd hit going from v2 back to v1.

**What you're suggesting works:**
- `wrote` keeps meaning the PIN's fingerprint, unchanged.
- Other credential types go in a new optional field. A record without it means nothing was written for those types.
- The store stays at version 1 and needs no migration. An older release can still read the store, because it never looks at the new field.

The one thing a downgrade costs is small. The old `remember` rebuilds each slot's record from scratch, so it drops the new field the first time it saves. After upgrading again, each password would be written once more on locks that hide their credentials. That's the same cost as today's "delete the store" recovery, but only for passwords and with no setup failure. PINs and owed releases are unaffected.

**What I'd do:** PR 1 never stores anything except a PIN, so it shouldn't touch the store's shape at all. In #1769, the change would be:
- Put `lock_store.py` back to `main`'s shape and version.
- Have `wrote(key, address)` read `wrote` only for PIN addresses.
- Remove `_Store`, `_per_type`, the migration tests and the "Downgrading" paragraph from the PR body.

PR 1 gets smaller and keeps a no-behavior-change refactor free of upgrade or downgrade consequences. The optional field for other types gets added in PR 2, where passwords first need it, and I'd add that to the carryover list.

Shall I make the change as a follow-up commit on #1769? I'd add a commit rather than amend, and push it after the tests and `prek` pass.

    # Keeping it current --------------------------------------------------------

    @callback
    def remember(
        self,
        key: str,
        lock: str,
        worker: LockWorker[CredentialAddress, Any],
        given_up_by: Callable[[int], str | None],
    ) -> None:
        """
        Take what ``worker`` knows of ``lock`` now; what it no longer tracks keeps its own.

        Per slot, each credential type the worker tracks is written over; a
        type it does not track keeps what was last written for it. A release
        is kept while it is still going, not once held: its repair brings it
        back. ``given_up_by`` names the entry that gave a slot up.
        """
        record = self._locks.get(key, {"answered": False, "slots": {}})
        slots = dict(record["slots"])
        tracked: defaultdict[int, list[tuple[CredentialAddress, Slot]]] = defaultdict(
            list
        )
        for address, slot in worker.slots.items():
            tracked[address.user_ref].append((address, slot))
        for number, held in tracked.items():
            wrote = dict(slots.get(str(number), {}).get("wrote", {}))
            for address, slot in held:
                if slot.wrote is None:
                    wrote.pop(address.credential_type.value, None)
                else:
                    wrote[address.credential_type.value] = slot.wrote
            saved: dict[str, Any] = {"wrote": wrote} if wrote else {}
            if any(slot.release and slot.hold is None for _, slot in held) and (
                by := given_up_by(number)
            ):
                saved["release"] = by
            if saved:
                slots[str(number)] = saved
            else:
                slots.pop(str(number), None)
        self._put(
            key,
            {
                **record,
                "entity_id": lock,
                "answered": worker.answered_ever,
                "slots": slots,
            },
        )

    # Keeping it current --------------------------------------------------------

    @callback
    def remember(
        self,
        key: str,
        lock: str,
        worker: LockWorker[CredentialAddress, Any],
        given_up_by: Callable[[int], str | None],
    ) -> None:
        """
        Take what ``worker`` knows of ``lock`` now; what it no longer tracks keeps its own.

        Per slot, each credential type the worker tracks is written over; a
        type it does not track keeps what was last written for it. A release
        is kept while it is still going, not once held: its repair brings it
        back. ``given_up_by`` names the entry that gave a slot up.
        """
        record = self._locks.get(key, {"answered": False, "slots": {}})
        slots = dict(record["slots"])
        tracked: defaultdict[int, list[tuple[CredentialAddress, Slot]]] = defaultdict(
            list
        )
        for address, slot in worker.slots.items():
            tracked[address.user_ref].append((address, slot))
        for number, held in tracked.items():
            wrote = dict(slots.get(str(number), {}).get("wrote", {}))
            for address, slot in held:
                if slot.wrote is None:
                    wrote.pop(address.credential_type.value, None)
                else:
                    wrote[address.credential_type.value] = slot.wrote
            saved: dict[str, Any] = {"wrote": wrote} if wrote else {}
            if any(slot.release and slot.hold is None for _, slot in held) and (
                by := given_up_by(number)
            ):
                saved["release"] = by
            if saved:
                slots[str(number)] = saved
            else:
                slots.pop(str(number), None)
        self._put(
            key,
            {
                **record,
                "entity_id": lock,
                "answered": worker.answered_ever,
                "slots": slots,
            },
        )

For PR 1, I'm thinking `wrote(key, address)` should only store PIN addresses, returning None for others, and `remember` groups by slot with PIN's wrote stored while release gets aggregated. Non-PIN addresses would silently store nothing in PR 1 since the adapter refuses them, with the optional field for that behavior deferred to PR 2.

Since grouping by slot is needed anyway to avoid one address's write overwriting another's within the same slot, I'm sketching remember to find the PIN entry per tracked number and build the saved dict from that.

I realize this drops a previously-stored PIN's wrote value if the worker only tracks the password for that slot now, so I need to pull from the existing stored data to preserve untracked types' values — checking if this level of care is warranted for PR 1 or overengineered, and whether the existing test for "remembering one type keeps the others" still holds under this logic.

I'm deciding against a generic dict-keyed-by-type approach since it's premature for the current PR, and I'll just go with the explicit version. I also need to revert the module docstring to match main's phrasing about tracking what was last written as the slot's PIN, then actually read the current file so I can prepare the edits.

1	"""
2	What the lock workers remember across a restart, in one Home Assistant Store.
3	
4	Per lock, keyed by the entity registry id its worker is bound to, so a rename
5	keeps it (#1442) and a device re-paired under the same entity id never finds
6	the old one's, with its entity id beside it: whether the lock has ever
7	answered, whether a read of it has ever described a slot (#1581; absent in a
8	record saved before, and then not known to), and per slot what was last
9	written for each credential type -- a keyed fingerprint or ``cleared``, never
10	the value -- and a release clear still owed, with the entry that gave the slot
11	up. What a slot holds is read again; counts, fights and holds start over (a
12	hold's repair outlives a restart on its own).
13	
14	Written a second after a change, and at Home Assistant's final write. Never
15	dropped on an unload (#1243): only when a release is done, a slot is let go
16	of for good, a lock leaves Lock Code Manager or an entry is deleted. A
17	record whose registry id is gone goes at the next start.
18	"""
19	
20	from collections import defaultdict
21	from collections.abc import Callable, Collection
22	from typing import Any, override
23	
24	from homeassistant.core import HomeAssistant, callback
25	from homeassistant.helpers import entity_registry as er
26	from homeassistant.helpers.storage import Store
27	
28	from ..const import DOMAIN
29	from ..model.credentials import CredentialAddress, CredentialType, pin_address
30	from ..sync.slot import CLEARED, Slot
31	from ..sync.worker import LockWorker
32	
33	STORE_KEY = f"{DOMAIN}.core"
34	STORE_VERSION = 2
35	SAVE_DELAY = 1.0
36	
37	Record = dict[str, Any]
38	
39	
40	class _Store(Store[dict[str, Any]]):
41	    """The core's store, moving older records to the current shape as it loads."""
42	
43	    @override
44	    async def _async_migrate_func(
45	        self, old_major_version: int, old_minor_version: int, old_data: dict[str, Any]
46	    ) -> dict[str, Any]:
47	        """Version 1 kept one fingerprint per slot: a PIN's."""
48	        locks = old_data.get("locks", {})
49	        if old_major_version < 2:
50	            locks = {
51	                key: {
52	                    **record,
53	                    "slots": {
54	                        number: _per_type(saved)
55	                        for number, saved in record["slots"].items()
56	                    },
57	                }
58	                for key, record in locks.items()
59	            }
60	        return {**old_data, "locks": locks}
61	
62	
63	def _per_type(saved: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
64	    """Return a version 1 slot record with what was written kept under PIN."""
65	    if "wrote" not in saved:
66	        return saved
67	    return {**saved, "wrote": {CredentialType.PIN.value: saved["wrote"]}}
68	
69	
70	class LockStore:
71	    """Each lock's record, under ``key``: the registry id its worker is bound to."""
72	
73	    def __init__(self, hass: HomeAssistant) -> None:
74	        """Start empty; ``async_load`` reads what was saved."""
75	        self._hass = hass
76	        self._store: Store[dict[str, Any]] = _Store(hass, STORE_VERSION, STORE_KEY)
77	        self._locks: dict[str, Record] = {}
78	
79	    async def async_load(self) -> None:
80	        """Read what was saved, each record under its lock's current entity id."""
81	        saved = await self._store.async_load() or {}
82	        self._locks = saved.get("locks", {})
83	        registry = er.async_get(self._hass)
84	        for key, record in self._locks.items():
85	            if (entity := registry.async_get(key)) is not None:
86	                record["entity_id"] = entity.entity_id
87	
88	    # What a lock's worker starts from ------------------------------------------
89	
90	    def wrote(self, key: str, address: CredentialAddress) -> str | None:
91	        """Return what was last written at ``address`` on the lock, if anything."""
92	        record = self._locks.get(key)
93	        if record is None:
94	            return None
95	        saved = record["slots"].get(str(address.user_ref), {})
96	        return saved.get("wrote", {}).get(address.credential_type.value)
97	
98	    def wrote_pin(self, key: str, slot: int) -> bool:
99	        """
100	        Return whether a PIN was what was last written to ``slot`` on the lock.
101	
102	        A slot only ever cleared never held Lock Code Manager's code.
103	        """
104	        return self.wrote(key, pin_address(slot)) not in (None, CLEARED)
105	
106	    def answered(self, key: str) -> bool:
107	        """Return whether the lock has ever answered."""
108	        record = self._locks.get(key)
109	        return record is not None and record["answered"]
110	
111	    def reports(self, key: str) -> bool:
112	        """Return whether a read of the lock has ever described a slot."""
113	        record = self._locks.get(key)
114	        return record is not None and record.get("reports", False)
115	
116	    def releases(self) -> list[tuple[str, int, str]]:
117	        """Return each release clear still owed: lock, slot, the entry that gave it up."""
118	        return [
119	            (record["entity_id"], int(slot), saved["release"])
120	            for record in self._locks.values()
121	            for slot, saved in record["slots"].items()
122	            if "release" in saved
123	        ]
124	
125	    # Keeping it current --------------------------------------------------------

53	                    "slots": {

I want to clean up the docstring wording so it reads more naturally -- describing that each slot stores what was last written as a PIN, either a keyed fingerprint or "cleared", never the raw PIN itself. This ensures that if the PIN-only filter were removed, the mutation would surface since the password slot's wrote value would incorrectly populate the pin field.

content.thinking:
This approach works: write to a new per-type key while falling back to the old "wrote" field for PIN if the new key is missing, then eventually drop the fallback. I'm checking that reads, writes, and downgrade behavior all stay consistent with this scheme.

I found an edge case though — if the new code stops writing the old "wrote" field, a downgraded old release could see a stale fingerprint and wrongly trust a PIN that's since changed on the lock, skipping a necessary rewrite. The fix is to have the new code actively drop the old "wrote" key when it writes the new one, so old code sees it as never-written and safely rewrites once.

Separately, I'm worried old code interpreting a missing or false "written" flag might skip clearing an LCM PIN on release, leaving stale PINs on the lock — similar to a past bug. And the question of when it's safe to delete the fallback shape conversion is really a migration problem: unmigrated slots keep the old shape until touched, so removing the fallback early risks breaking installs that skip versions, which is exactly why major-version migrations exist in the first place.

Comparing this against my own proposal — keeping `wrote` as the PIN field and adding an optional field for others — mine avoids needing a fallback or later cleanup and keeps downgrades fully safe, including PIN state, whereas the uniform-shape approach requires fallback code, eventual cleanup, and loses PIN info on downgrade. I should check how `wrote_pin` is actually used on release in the current main branch so I can state the downgrade tradeoff precisely before answering the user's "why can't we" question.

I think yes, this works without a version bump: read the new key, falling back to the old field for PIN compatibility. But I should also flag that we need to stop writing the old field once the new key is adopted, since a stale fallback could be trusted incorrectly after a downgrade and cause the PIN to be lost.

Also, deleting the fallback entirely later only becomes safe once every stored record has actually been migrated to the new shape, and slots not actively tracked by the worker would never get converted -- which really amounts to a migration pass, the same problem the version bump was meant to solve. My preference is to keep the existing field for PIN specifically and add a separate optional field for other types in PR 2, avoiding any fallback or removal step and keeping downgrades fully safe, even though it makes the record slightly asymmetric -- though I'll let the user weigh in since my local edit already implements this approach uncommitted and untested.

content.text:
Yes, a fallback works, and it also avoids the version bump. But compared with keeping `wrote` as the PIN's key, it costs more in two places:

**1. Deleting the fallback later is a migration with extra steps.** Records only move to the new key when `remember` rewrites them, and `remember` only rewrites slots the worker still tracks. A slot nobody tracks any more, such as one still owed a release clear, keeps the old `wrote` until something converts it. So before the fallback can go, we need a conversion pass on load, which is a migration. Even then, anyone upgrading straight from before PR 1 to the release that dropped the fallback loses their fingerprints. HA's version bump exists to make that conversion in one place, once.

**2. Downgrades get worse, not better.** Once the new key exists, the old `wrote` either keeps being written or doesn't:
- **If it's kept in step**, every write goes to two keys until the cleanup. That is the asymmetric record again, plus the fallback code.
- **If it's left as it was**, it goes stale. After a downgrade, the old release trusts a fingerprint from before the upgrade. Set a PIN back to that older value, and a lock that hides its codes is never rewritten, even though it holds something else.
- **If it's removed when the new key is written**, the old release sees no record at all. Each hidden PIN is written again once, which is harmless. But `wrote_pin` also returns false, and it feeds `release(written=…)` (`runtime.py:975`), which tells a provider whether a PIN on that slot is Lock Code Manager's when a slot is given up. A downgrade would then change how releases behave, which is the kind of problem we're trying to avoid.

Keeping `wrote` as the PIN's key has none of these problems. There's no fallback, nothing to delete later, and a downgrade keeps working fully, because the old code reads exactly what the new code writes. In PR 2, passwords get a new optional field that older releases simply ignore. The only cost is that the PIN is stored differently from the other types. I think that's justified: the PIN was the only type when the store was first designed, and other types are additions.

I'd still go with keeping `wrote`, but it's your call.

## Proposed change

The first of four PRs toward password credentials. It re-keys the sync engine from a bare slot number to a credential address, `(slot, credential type)`, and changes no behavior: every address is a PIN for now.

- The sync engine (`sync/`: worker, port and registry) is now generic over its key, because `sync/` may not import `model/`. The integration keys it by `CredentialAddress`. The worker never looks inside a key.
- An entry still owns a whole slot. The registry is told which slot a key is in (`slot_of`), so claiming, giving up and letting go of a slot act on every credential type in it. Letting go never drops a clear another entry gave up and that is still being sent.
- The provider adapter turns an address back into today's slot-based provider calls. Any other credential type is refused before anything reaches the lock.
- The lock store keeps what was last written per credential type under a new `wrote_by_type` key, and keeps writing the PIN's under `wrote` as before. The store stays at version 1, with no migration:
  - A record without `wrote_by_type` is read as the PIN's alone. That covers records saved before this change, and any record saved by an older release after a downgrade.
  - An older release reads only `wrote`, which always holds the current PIN's fingerprint, so downgrading keeps working.
  - The fingerprint itself is unchanged, so no lock is written again after the upgrade.
- Diagnostics nest each lock's worker slots by credential type: `slots["3"]["pin"]`.

I pushed the store change to #1769 as a follow-up commit, `5770f326`. The store stays at version 1, and each slot's record now writes both keys:

```json
"1": {"wrote": "<pin fp>", "wrote_by_type": {"pin": "<pin fp>"}, "release": "…"}
```

- **Reading:** a record that has `wrote_by_type` uses it. A record without it is read as the PIN's alone, taken from `wrote`. That covers records saved before this change and any record an older release saves after a downgrade.
- **Writing:** `remember` writes per-type fingerprints into `wrote_by_type` and keeps types the worker doesn't track. It also writes the PIN's fingerprint to `wrote`, and only the PIN's; a slot holding only a password gets no `wrote`.
- **Removed:** the `_Store` subclass, the migration and the "Downgrading" paragraph in the PR body. The PR body's store bullet now describes the two keys.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Writing both keys holds up after a downgrade because an older release rebuilds every slot record it saves from scratch. So `wrote_by_type` is either missing, and we fall back to `wrote`, which is current, or was left alone by the older release, and agrees with `wrote`. The two can never disagree.
- It works without any version number because of the reading rule: a record without `wrote_by_type` is read as the PIN's alone. That one rule covers both records saved before this change and records saved after a downgrade.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**Verification:**
- Store, init, diagnostics and runtime tests: 245 passed.
- Mutation checks: I broke each new behavior in turn (the `wrote` copy, the fallback to `wrote`, the copy being the PIN's only, keeping untracked types) and confirmed each one fails tests. The file was restored afterwards.
- `prek` and mypy pass.
- Full parallel run (`-n auto`): 3370 passed and 3 failed. The failures are tests that measure real elapsed time between paced writes (`TestPacing`, the binary sensor paced test, the harness pacing test). Run on their own, the 4 tests in those groups pass, and none of them touches the store. These failures could hit CI if it runs tests in parallel on a busy runner.

I added the decision to the PR 2 carryover file: keep writing `wrote` for the foreseeable future, and don't bump the store version for passwords. It's in the password-design memory too.

The user now suggests naming the key "state," but that feels ambiguous given Home Assistant's own entity states—it could be confused with the lock's actual state rather than what LCM last wrote to the slot. Since the store deliberately doesn't track what the slot currently holds, "state" risks implying something the data doesn't actually represent.

I should push back and recommend sticking with `fingerprints`, or `written` if they want the `cleared` nit addressed—but keep it short and wait for confirmation before changing anything. First I should mention the rename push (06d8e31d) since I haven't reported that yet.

content.text:
The rename to `fingerprints` is pushed in `06d8e31d`. Store and diagnostics tests pass, `prek` and mypy pass, and the PR body, carryover file and memory all use the new name.

I'd not use `state`, for two reasons:

- **It implies something the store deliberately doesn't keep.** The module docstring says "What a slot holds is read again": what the lock currently holds is never stored. The record holds only what Lock Code Manager last wrote there, which it uses to decide whether to trust a lock that hides its codes. `state` reads like the lock's own state, and someone would reasonably start treating it as a cache of the lock. That's the confusion between what was observed and what is trusted that we spent the optimistic/confirmed work separating.
- **"State" already has a meaning in Home Assistant.** In this codebase, `state` usually means an entity's state in `hass.states`. A `state` key in the store would get confused with that in grep results and in reviews.

If what bothers you is that `cleared` isn't a fingerprint, `written` is the accurate name: what Lock Code Manager last wrote, per type, either a fingerprint or `cleared`. It also matches the `wrote()` and `wrote_pin()` reads.

My order of preference is `fingerprints` (as pushed) or `written`, and either is a one-commit rename. Do you want `written`, or keep it as is?

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** This should be run in a dedicated worktree (created by brainstorming skill).

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## No Placeholders

Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** — never write them:
- "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
- "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
- "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
- "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code — the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
- Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
- References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task

## Remember
- Exact file paths always
- Complete code in every step — if a step changes code, show the code
- Exact commands with expected output
- DRY, YAGNI, TDD, frequent commits

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags — any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan, offer execution choice:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Two execution options:**

**1. Subagent-Driven (recommended)** - I dispatch a fresh subagent per task, review between tasks, fast iteration

**2. Inline Execution** - Execute tasks in this session using executing-plans, batch execution with checkpoints

**Which approach?"**

**If Subagent-Driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

**If Inline Execution chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review

# Password credentials

**Date:** 2026-10-22. **Status:** approved 2026-10-23.
**Base:** `origin/main` at `ce1e1088` (clean-room core merged in #1702).
**Builds on:** `2026-08-16-user-centric-credential-model-design.md` (sub-project C, never specced until now) and the 2026-09-16 multi-credential decisions (memory `project_multi_credential_types_plan`).

## Goal

A user can hold a password as well as, or instead of, a PIN. Lock Code Manager writes it to every lock in the entry that takes passwords and keeps it in sync there, the way it does PINs today.

## Scope

In:

- Password as a second managed credential type, end to end: sync core, storage, Z-Wave and Virtual providers, entities, config, services, websocket, slot card, add-user card and lock card.
- Making the core type-generic, so that RFID and NFC can later be added as data, not as structure.

Out:

- RFID, NFC and biometrics.
- A pattern on the PIN entity (see "Text entities").
- Showing or editing unmanaged passwords on the lock card.
- User Code CC locks whose keypad accepts non-digit characters. The driver uses the Password type for these (`node-zwave-js AccessControl.ts:1598`), and they may be invisible to Lock Code Manager today. Follow-up issue.

## Decisions

| # | Decision |
|---|---|
| 1 | Passwords are printable ASCII, 0x20–0x7E, spaces included. The Z-Wave spec requires passwords to travel as UTF-16 big endian (CC:0083.01.0A.11.021) and counts Credential Length in bytes (.0A.11.014/.015). 2026A's worked example gives a 17-character password a length of 34. Every printable ASCII character is exactly 2 bytes, so the per-lock length check compares `2 × len(password)` against the lock's limits. |
| 2 | The sync core is keyed by `CredentialAddress(slot, type)`. There is still one worker per lock. |
| 3 | Release stays per slot: one release removes every type Lock Code Manager wrote for the slot. |
| 4 | A slot needs at least one credential of any type. Clearing a credential disables the slot only when no other credential remains. A stored value counts even if no current lock takes its type. |
| 5 | On Z-Wave, the password index is allocated by the provider: it finds the tagged user's password wherever it is, or else takes the lowest password index no user holds. PIN keeps following the slot. |
| 6 | Credential text entities set no `pattern`, `native_min` or `native_max`. One validator and the coordinator's per-lock length check are the only gates, and their errors never contain the value. |
| 7 | Passwords are not whitespace-stripped. PINs keep `vol.Strip`. |
| 8 | Slot card: tabs per type over one value field, each tab's dot showing that type's sync state. Tabs appear only when the entry offers more than one type. |
| 9 | Lock card: tabs per type. The PIN tab is today's card. The Password tab lists managed users' passwords on that lock. |
| 10 | Carried from 2026-09-16: an entry's available types are the union across its locks. A type no longer offered keeps its stored value, and its entity is removed. Per-type in-sync sensors are disabled by default. Duplicates are refused within a type and allowed across types. The generator covers passwords. |

## Sync core

`CredentialAddress(user_ref, credential_type)` already exists (`model/credentials.py`). It becomes the key everywhere in `sync/`. `sync/` may not import `model/` (`tests/test_architecture.py`), so the worker, port and registry are generic over their key, and the HA layer instantiates them with `CredentialAddress`. The registry is told the slot a key belongs to (`slot_of`), because entries own slots, not addresses. The existing `tests/sync/` suite keeps its integer keys unchanged, which makes it a strict oracle for the re-key (amended 2026-10-23 while planning PR 1):

- `LockWorker.slots: dict[CredentialAddress, Slot]`. `want`, `forget`, `resume`, `status`, `syncing` and `push` take an address.
- `LockPort.read(addresses) -> Mapping[CredentialAddress, Reading]` and `LockPort.write(address, value) -> bool | None`.
- `sync/slot.py` stays a single-value state machine. `Holds.pin` becomes `Holds.value`, `Want` stays `str | None`, and `Holds.__repr__` keeps masking.
- `sync/registry.py` and `ha/adapter.py` re-key to match. The adapter turns an address into the provider call for that type.
- Release is per slot. When a slot leaves the entry, the worker sends one release for the slot. The provider removes every credential Lock Code Manager wrote to that slot's user, then the user only if it holds nothing else.

**Managed addresses are per lock:** `{CredentialAddress(slot, t) for t in lock.capabilities.credential_types ∩ MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES}`. This covers every type the lock takes, not only the types the user has a value for. A user with no password still gets a password address on a password lock, with want `None`, so a password cleared or never set is kept cleared, the same way an empty PIN is kept cleared today. A lock that doesn't take password never gets a password address, so the aggregate `in_sync` on that lock ignores the type. This fixes the global `managed_addresses()` gap found in the #1572 review. Recompute when a lock is added or removed and when capabilities refresh.

`MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES` becomes `{PIN, PASSWORD}`.

## Storage

`ha/lock_store.py`, `STORE_VERSION` 1 → 2.

- v1 slot record: `{"wrote": <fingerprint|cleared>, …release fields}`.
- v2 slot record: `{"wrote": {"pin": <fingerprint|cleared>, "password": REDACTED, …release fields}`.
- Migration: move v1 `wrote` under `"pin"`. Release fields stay at slot level.
- The fingerprint stays `fingerprint(value, salt)`. Credential values are never persisted. (Amended 2026-10-23 while planning PR 1: a type-salted fingerprint would leave every migrated v1 fingerprint unmatched, so each PIN on a lock that hides its codes would be rewritten once after the upgrade. The record already keeps each type under its own key, so salting with the type adds nothing.)

The Store migration is the only one-way step. Downgrading leaves a v2 Store the old version can't read, and HA's Store versioning is there to refuse that.

## Configuration and the credential-required rule

- The user subentry gets an optional `password` (absent means none), and setup YAML gets `password:` per user. No config-entry migration is needed.
- The rule changes in four places:
  - `ha/slot_coordinator.py:294`: clearing any credential disables an enabled slot only if no other credential remains.
  - `ha/slot_coordinator.py:355`: enabling is refused only when the user has no credential of any type. `PinRequiredError` becomes `CredentialRequiredError`.
  - `config_flow.py:84-93, 422`: `_slot_enabled_without_pin` becomes `_slot_enabled_without_credential`, which checks every managed type's field.
  - Repair `pin_required` becomes `credential_required`. Update `switch.py:62`, `ha/services.py:451`, `repairs.py:179` and `__init__.py:1220`. At startup, delete any leftover `pin_required_*` issue.

## Providers

**Z-Wave (`providers/zwave_js.py`)**

- **Capabilities:** also report `PASSWORD` from the same `supported_credential_types` read: slot count, min/max length and `supports_learn`. A lock without password is unchanged.
- **Read `(slot, password)`:** find the user tagged `lcm:<slot>:` and return its password credential, wherever it sits, as `Holds`, `MASKED` or `EMPTY`.
- **Write:** overwrite the tagged user's password credential in place. If it has none, use the lowest password index **no user on the lock holds**, taken from the user list read just before the write, so vendor-app credentials are never overwritten. Create the user on the first write of either type, as PIN does now.
- **Clear:** delete that password credential only. The user stays.
- **Release:** delete every credential Lock Code Manager wrote to the user (PIN and password), then the user only if it holds nothing else.
- **No free index:** raise `LockOperationUnsupported`, naming the lock and its password slot count. The address holds as `CANT_SET`.

**Virtual:** already advertises every type. Its password is keyed by slot.

**Base (`providers/_base.py`):** `_assert_slot_within_capacity` stays PIN-only, because password doesn't follow the slot.

**Everyone else:** no change. Password support was checked against each provider's standard or code (2026-10-22):

| Provider | Credential types | Password? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Z-Wave (User Credential CC) | PIN, Password, RFID, BLE, NFC, UWB, biometrics | Yes | AWG 2026A spec, Table "Credential Type Encoding"; node-zwave-js `_Types.ts:1657` |
| Matter | ProgrammingPIN, PIN, RFID, Fingerprint, FingerVein, Face, Aliro ×3 | No | Matter 1.7 data model `DoorLock.xml:195-234` |
| ZHA, Z2M | Zigbee Cluster Library Door Lock: PIN, RFID; only PIN can be written | No | zigpy `closures.py`; zha `lock/__init__.py:156-182`; zigbee-herdsman-converters `exposes.ts`, `toZigbee.ts` |
| Schlage | One access code, `^\d{4,8}$` | No | pyschlage `code.py:164-188`; HA `schlage/__init__.py:37` |
| Akuvox | `private_pin` (4–8 digits), `card_code` | No | pylocal-akuvox `users.py:19-47`; local_akuvox `validation.py:53-65` |
| zwave-js-ui MQTT | Legacy User Code CC `userCode` | Not through this provider | LCM `providers/zwave_js_ui.py` |

**Z-Wave is blocked upstream.** node-zwave-js writes string credentials as UTF-8 (`AccessControl.ts:1140`) and reads passwords back as UTF-8 (`UserCredentialCC.ts:82`). The spec requires UTF-16BE, so a compliant lock would decode `abcd` (4 UTF-8 bytes) as 2 unrelated characters. Grizzly (`user_credential.ex:159-166`) encodes UTF-16 as the spec requires. The Silicon Labs reference firmware validates only PIN data (`cc_user_credential_validation.c:87-110`), so it would store UTF-8 bytes without rejecting them. PR 4 waits for the driver fix (zwave-js/zwave-js#9396).

**Minimum driver version (decided 2026-10-23: raise it for everyone).** HA's Z-Wave integration checks only the server schema version (`zwave_js_server` `MIN_SERVER_SCHEMA_VERSION`), and a bug-fix driver release doesn't change the schema. So a minimum HA version can't guarantee a driver. PR 4 adds a setup-time check: compare `client.version.driver_version` against the first release containing #9396. If the driver is older, refuse to set up the lock with an error naming the required version. This applies to every Z-Wave lock, not only ones with passwords. It's a breaking change for users on older drivers, so the PR gets a Breaking Change section. The same check replaces the "guaranteed by the integration's minimum Home Assistant version" claim in `zwave_js.py:200-203` about 15.24.3.

HA core's `zwave_js/lock_helpers.py:236` compares `len(str)` against the byte limits and has the same gap.

## Entities and validation

**Text entities (`text.py`)**

- Split `LockCodeManagerText` into `LockCodeManagerNameText` and `LockCodeManagerCredentialText(credential_type)`, with subclasses `PinText` and `PasswordText`. All credential entities use `TextMode.PASSWORD`.
- `async_set_value` calls `coordinator.async_request_credential_update(type, value)`.
- No `pattern`, `native_min` or `native_max`. HA's own errors embed the cleartext value (`homeassistant/components/text/__init__.py:73-86`), and it re-checks them when rendering state (`:162-178`).
- Credential entities exist for the entry's available types. They're added and removed as that union changes.

**Validator:** `model/credentials.py: validate_credential_value(type, value)` checks the character set: digits for PIN, 0x20–0x7E for password. It's called from the coordinator, the config flow, `add_user`, `set_credential` and the setup YAML schema. Error text names the rule and never the value. For example: "Password may only contain letters, digits, symbols and spaces".

**Length:** `_validate_credential_length(value, type)` (`slot_coordinator.py:303`) is called for password against password-capable locks only. Its message already names each lock and its range.

**Labels:** add `"password": "Password"` to `CREDENTIAL_LABELS` (`const.py:210`) and `ts/const.ts`, which a contract test checks. That gives:
- the `password_in_sync` sensor, disabled by default (`binary_sensor.py:163`);
- password in `SENSITIVE_ENTITY_KEYS`, so diagnostics redact it;
- password in the event entity's types (`event.py:122`).

**Duplicates:** refuse a password another user in the entry already holds.

**Masking:** `mask_pin` becomes `mask_credential`, used in every log line that carries a value.

**Generator:** `generate_pin` becomes `generate_credential(type, length)`. For password it uses the printable ASCII set, at a length inside every password-capable lock's range in the entry.

## Services and websocket

- `add_user` gets `password`. `set_credential` and `clear_credential` accept `password` once it's in `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES` (`ha/services.py:186`).
- `subscribe_code_slot` gets `available_types` and `credentials: {<type>: {value | length, in_sync, state}}`.
- `subscribe_lock_codes` keeps `slots` as the PIN view and adds `credentials.password`: one entry per managed user holding a password on this lock (slot, name, entry, value or length, in_sync).
- These payloads are internal. The card ships with the integration.
- Before release, check blueprints and `services.yaml` for PIN-only assumptions.

## Cards

- **Slot card (`ts/slot-card.ts`):**
  - The type tabs sit between the name and the value row. Each tab's dot shows that type's sync state: in sync, or pending or held.
  - Only the value field changes per tab. The name, enable switch, conditions and lock list stay the same.
  - The edit input sets `inputmode` per type (today it's hard-coded `numeric` at `:607`) and shows a length hint from the lock ranges.
  - With one available type, the card renders exactly as it does today.
- **Add-user card (`ts/add-user-card.ts`):** the same tabs on the credential input, with a per-type generator.
- **Lock card (`ts/lock-codes-card.ts`):** the type tabs appear when the lock takes more than one managed type. The PIN tab is today's card. The Password tab has one chip per managed user, with no empty-position ranges and no unmanaged editing.

## Testing

Order: property, then end-to-end, then integration, then unit.

- **Property:** the Hypothesis stateful sync property runs over `(slot, type)` addresses with both types. Invariants:
  - each type converges independently;
  - a lock without password never gets a password address;
  - after release, no Lock Code Manager credential remains on the lock.
- **End-to-end:** Virtual for all types. Z-Wave uses a **sourced** node dump of a User Credential CC lock that advertises password, cited by source. If none exists, stop and ask rather than make one up.
- **Leak test:** submit an invalid value carrying a unique marker. Assert the marker appears in neither the raised error nor `caplog`.
- **Mutation checks:** the per-lock address filter, release removing the password, the "lowest index no user holds" rule, and "a clear disables only when no credential remains".

## PR order

Each PR is reviewed on its own. The release ships after PR 4. Its driver minimum is a Breaking Change, so the version bump follows the project's breaking-change rule.

1. **Core re-key to `CredentialAddress`, plus Store v2.** No behavior change, since every address is PIN, so the existing suite and properties are a strict oracle.
2. **Password in the model and HA layer:** `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES`, per-lock addresses, the credential-required rule, the validator, the text entity split, config and services, `CREDENTIAL_LABELS`. Exercised on Virtual.
3. **Cards:** slot card, add-user card, lock card.
4. **Z-Wave provider**, after a driver release contains zwave-js/zwave-js#9396: the minimum driver version check, capabilities, read, allocation on write, clear, release. Breaking Change: Z-Wave locks need that driver release.

PRs 1–3 ship Password on Virtual only, so they can merge before the driver fix. The release goes out with PR 4.

## Open items

- node-zwave-js password encoding: UTF-8 today, the spec requires UTF-16BE (blocks PR 4). HA core's `lock_helpers` length check needs the same fix.
- The sourced Z-Wave User Credential CC dump with password capability (blocks PR 4 tests).
- The follow-up issue for User Code CC alphanumeric locks.

- Making the core type-generic, so that RFID and NFC can later be added as data, not as structure.

Out:

- RFID, NFC and biometrics.
- A pattern on the PIN entity (see "Text entities").
- Showing or editing unmanaged passwords on the lock card.
- User Code CC locks whose keypad accepts non-digit characters. The driver uses the Password type for these (`node-zwave-js AccessControl.ts:1598`), and they may be invisible to Lock Code Manager today. Follow-up issue.

## Decisions

| # | Decision |
|---|---|
| 1 | Passwords are printable ASCII, 0x20–0x7E, spaces included. The Z-Wave spec requires passwords to travel as UTF-16 big endian (CC:0083.01.0A.11.021) and counts Credential Length in bytes (.0A.11.014/.015). 2026A's worked example gives a 17-character password a length of 34. Every printable ASCII character is exactly 2 bytes, so the per-lock length check compares `2 × len(password)` against the lock's limits. |
| 2 | The sync core is keyed by `CredentialAddress(slot, type)`. There is still one worker per lock. |
| 3 | Release stays per slot: one release removes every type Lock Code Manager wrote for the slot. |
| 4 | A slot needs at least one credential of any type. Clearing a credential disables the slot only when no other credential remains. A stored value counts even if no current lock takes its type. |
| 5 | On Z-Wave, the password index is allocated by the provider: it finds the tagged user's password wherever it is, or else takes the lowest password index no user holds. PIN keeps following the slot. |
| 6 | Credential text entities set no `pattern`, `native_min` or `native_max`. One validator and the coordinator's per-lock length check are the only gates, and their errors never contain the value. |
| 7 | Passwords are not whitespace-stripped. PINs keep `vol.Strip`. |
| 8 | Slot card: tabs per type over one value field, each tab's dot showing that type's sync state. Tabs appear only when the entry offers more than one type. |
| 9 | Lock card: tabs per type. The PIN tab is today's card. The Password tab lists managed users' passwords on that lock. |
| 10 | Carried from 2026-09-16: an entry's available types are the union across its locks. A type no longer offered keeps its stored value, and its entity is removed. Per-type in-sync sensors are disabled by default. Duplicates are refused within a type and allowed across types. The generator covers passwords. |

## Sync core

`CredentialAddress(user_ref, credential_type)` already exists (`model/credentials.py`). It becomes the key everywhere in `sync/`. `sync/` may not import `model/` (`tests/test_architecture.py`), so the worker, port and registry are generic over their key, and the HA layer instantiates them with `CredentialAddress`. The registry is told the slot a key belongs to (`slot_of`), because entries own slots, not addresses. The existing `tests/sync/` suite keeps its integer keys unchanged, which makes it a strict oracle for the re-key (amended 2026-10-23 while planning PR 1):

- `LockWorker.slots: dict[CredentialAddress, Slot]`. `want`, `forget`, `resume`, `status`, `syncing` and `push` take an address.
- `LockPort.read(addresses) -> Mapping[CredentialAddress, Reading]` and `LockPort.write(address, value) -> bool | None`.
- `sync/slot.py` stays a single-value state machine. `Holds.pin` becomes `Holds.value`, `Want` stays `str | None`, and `Holds.__repr__` keeps masking.
- `sync/registry.py` and `ha/adapter.py` re-key to match. The adapter turns an address into the provider call for that type.
- Release is per slot. When a slot leaves the entry, the worker sends one release for the slot. The provider removes every credential Lock Code Manager wrote to that slot's user, then the user only if it holds nothing else.

**Managed addresses are per lock:** `{CredentialAddress(slot, t) for t in lock.capabilities.credential_types ∩ MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES}`. This covers every type the lock takes, not only the types the user has a value for. A user with no password still gets a password address on a password lock, with want `None`, so a password cleared or never set is kept cleared, the same way an empty PIN is kept cleared today. A lock that doesn't take password never gets a password address, so the aggregate `in_sync` on that lock ignores the type. This fixes the global `managed_addresses()` gap found in the #1572 review. Recompute when a lock is added or removed and when capabilities refresh.

`MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES` becomes `{PIN, PASSWORD}`.

## Storage

`ha/lock_store.py`, `STORE_VERSION` 1 → 2.

- v1 slot record: `{"wrote": <fingerprint|cleared>, …release fields}`.
- v2 slot record: `{"wrote": {"pin": <fingerprint|cleared>, "password": REDACTED, …release fields}`.
- Migration: move v1 `wrote` under `"pin"`. Release fields stay at slot level.
- The fingerprint stays `fingerprint(value, salt)`. Credential values are never persisted. (Amended 2026-10-23 while planning PR 1: a type-salted fingerprint would leave every migrated v1 fingerprint unmatched, so each PIN on a lock that hides its codes would be rewritten once after the upgrade. The record already keeps each type under its own key, so salting with the type adds nothing.)

The Store migration is the only one-way step. Downgrading leaves a v2 Store the old version can't read, and HA's Store versioning is there to refuse that.

## Configuration and the credential-required rule

- The user subentry gets an optional `password` (absent means none), and setup YAML gets `password:` per user. No config-entry migration is needed.
- The rule changes in four places:
  - `ha/slot_coordinator.py:294`: clearing any credential disables an enabled slot only if no other credential remains.
  - `ha/slot_coordinator.py:355`: enabling is refused only when the user has no credential of any type. `PinRequiredError` becomes `CredentialRequiredError`.
  - `config_flow.py:84-93, 422`: `_slot_enabled_without_pin` becomes `_slot_enabled_without_credential`, which checks every managed type's field.
  - Repair `pin_required` becomes `credential_required`. Update `switch.py:62`, `ha/services.py:451`, `repairs.py:179` and `__init__.py:1220`. At startup, delete any leftover `pin_required_*` issue.

## Providers

**Z-Wave (`providers/zwave_js.py`)**

- **Capabilities:** also report `PASSWORD` from the same `supported_credential_types` read: slot count, min/max length and `supports_learn`. A lock without password is unchanged.
- **Read `(slot, password)`:** find the user tagged `lcm:<slot>:` and return its password credential, wherever it sits, as `Holds`, `MASKED` or `EMPTY`.
- **Write:** overwrite the tagged user's password credential in place. If it has none, use the lowest password index **no user on the lock holds**, taken from the user list read just before the write, so vendor-app credentials are never overwritten. Create the user on the first write of either type, as PIN does now.
- **Clear:** delete that password credential only. The user stays.
- **Release:** delete every credential Lock Code Manager wrote to the user (PIN and password), then the user only if it holds nothing else.
- **No free index:** raise `LockOperationUnsupported`, naming the lock and its password slot count. The address holds as `CANT_SET`.

**Virtual:** already advertises every type. Its password is keyed by slot.

**Base (`providers/_base.py`):** `_assert_slot_within_capacity` stays PIN-only, because password doesn't follow the slot.

**Everyone else:** no change. Password support was checked against each provider's standard or code (2026-10-22):

| Provider | Credential types | Password? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Z-Wave (User Credential CC) | PIN, Password, RFID, BLE, NFC, UWB, biometrics | Yes | AWG 2026A spec, Table "Credential Type Encoding"; node-zwave-js `_Types.ts:1657` |
| Matter | ProgrammingPIN, PIN, RFID, Fingerprint, FingerVein, Face, Aliro ×3 | No | Matter 1.7 data model `DoorLock.xml:195-234` |
| ZHA, Z2M | Zigbee Cluster Library Door Lock: PIN, RFID; only PIN can be written | No | zigpy `closures.py`; zha `lock/__init__.py:156-182`; zigbee-herdsman-converters `exposes.ts`, `toZigbee.ts` |
| Schlage | One access code, `^\d{4,8}$` | No | pyschlage `code.py:164-188`; HA `schlage/__init__.py:37` |
| Akuvox | `private_pin` (4–8 digits), `card_code` | No | pylocal-akuvox `users.py:19-47`; local_akuvox `validation.py:53-65` |
| zwave-js-ui MQTT | Legacy User Code CC `userCode` | Not through this provider | LCM `providers/zwave_js_ui.py` |

**Z-Wave is blocked upstream.** node-zwave-js writes string credentials as UTF-8 (`AccessControl.ts:1140`) and reads passwords back as UTF-8 (`UserCredentialCC.ts:82`). The spec requires UTF-16BE, so a compliant lock would decode `abcd` (4 UTF-8 bytes) as 2 unrelated characters. Grizzly (`user_credential.ex:159-166`) encodes UTF-16 as the spec requires. The Silicon Labs reference firmware validates only PIN data (`cc_user_credential_validation.c:87-110`), so it would store UTF-8 bytes without rejecting them. PR 4 waits for the driver fix (zwave-js/zwave-js#9396).

**Minimum driver version (decided 2026-10-23: raise it for everyone).** HA's Z-Wave integration checks only the server schema version (`zwave_js_server` `MIN_SERVER_SCHEMA_VERSION`), and a bug-fix driver release doesn't change the schema. So a minimum HA version can't guarantee a driver. PR 4 adds a setup-time check: compare `client.version.driver_version` against the first release containing #9396. If the driver is older, refuse to set up the lock with an error naming the required version. This applies to every Z-Wave lock, not only ones with passwords. It's a breaking change for users on older drivers, so the PR gets a Breaking Change section. The same check replaces the "guaranteed by the integration's minimum Home Assistant version" claim in `zwave_js.py:200-203` about 15.24.3.

HA core's `zwave_js/lock_helpers.py:236` compares `len(str)` against the byte limits and has the same gap.

## Entities and validation

**Text entities (`text.py`)**

- Split `LockCodeManagerText` into `LockCodeManagerNameText` and `LockCodeManagerCredentialText(credential_type)`, with subclasses `PinText` and `PasswordText`. All credential entities use `TextMode.PASSWORD`.
- `async_set_value` calls `coordinator.async_request_credential_update(type, value)`.
- No `pattern`, `native_min` or `native_max`. HA's own errors embed the cleartext value (`homeassistant/components/text/__init__.py:73-86`), and it re-checks them when rendering state (`:162-178`).
- Credential entities exist for the entry's available types. They're added and removed as that union changes.

**Validator:** `model/credentials.py: validate_credential_value(type, value)` checks the character set: digits for PIN, 0x20–0x7E for password. It's called from the coordinator, the config flow, `add_user`, `set_credential` and the setup YAML schema. Error text names the rule and never the value. For example: "Password may only contain letters, digits, symbols and spaces".

**Length:** `_validate_credential_length(value, type)` (`slot_coordinator.py:303`) is called for password against password-capable locks only. Its message already names each lock and its range.

**Labels:** add `"password": "Password"` to `CREDENTIAL_LABELS` (`const.py:210`) and `ts/const.ts`, which a contract test checks. That gives:
- the `password_in_sync` sensor, disabled by default (`binary_sensor.py:163`);
- password in `SENSITIVE_ENTITY_KEYS`, so diagnostics redact it;
- password in the event entity's types (`event.py:122`).

**Duplicates:** refuse a password another user in the entry already holds.

**Masking:** `mask_pin` becomes `mask_credential`, used in every log line that carries a value.

**Generator:** `generate_pin` becomes `generate_credential(type, length)`. For password it uses the printable ASCII set, at a length inside every password-capable lock's range in the entry.

## Services and websocket

- `add_user` gets `password`. `set_credential` and `clear_credential` accept `password` once it's in `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES` (`ha/services.py:186`).
- `subscribe_code_slot` gets `available_types` and `credentials: {<type>: {value | length, in_sync, state}}`.
- `subscribe_lock_codes` keeps `slots` as the PIN view and adds `credentials.password`: one entry per managed user holding a password on this lock (slot, name, entry, value or length, in_sync).
- These payloads are internal. The card ships with the integration.
- Before release, check blueprints and `services.yaml` for PIN-only assumptions.

## Cards

- **Slot card (`ts/slot-card.ts`):**
  - The type tabs sit between the name and the value row. Each tab's dot shows that type's sync state: in sync, or pending or held.
  - Only the value field changes per tab. The name, enable switch, conditions and lock list stay the same.
  - The edit input sets `inputmode` per type (today it's hard-coded `numeric` at `:607`) and shows a length hint from the lock ranges.
  - With one available type, the card renders exactly as it does today.
- **Add-user card (`ts/add-user-card.ts`):** the same tabs on the credential input, with a per-type generator.
- **Lock card (`ts/lock-codes-card.ts`):** the type tabs appear when the lock takes more than one managed type. The PIN tab is today's card. The Password tab has one chip per managed user, with no empty-position ranges and no unmanaged editing.

## Testing

Order: property, then end-to-end, then integration, then unit.

- **Property:** the Hypothesis stateful sync property runs over `(slot, type)` addresses with both types. Invariants:
  - each type converges independently;
  - a lock without password never gets a password address;
  - after release, no Lock Code Manager credential remains on the lock.
- **End-to-end:** Virtual for all types. Z-Wave uses a **sourced** node dump of a User Credential CC lock that advertises password, cited by source. If none exists, stop and ask rather than make one up.
- **Leak test:** submit an invalid value carrying a unique marker. Assert the marker appears in neither the raised error nor `caplog`.
- **Mutation checks:** the per-lock address filter, release removing the password, the "lowest index no user holds" rule, and "a clear disables only when no credential remains".

## PR order

Each PR is reviewed on its own. The release ships after PR 4. Its driver minimum is a Breaking Change, so the version bump follows the project's breaking-change rule.

1. **Core re-key to `CredentialAddress`, plus Store v2.** No behavior change, since every address is PIN, so the existing suite and properties are a strict oracle.
2. **Password in the model and HA layer:** `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES`, per-lock addresses, the credential-required rule, the validator, the text entity split, config and services, `CREDENTIAL_LABELS`. Exercised on Virtual.
3. **Cards:** slot card, add-user card, lock card.
4. **Z-Wave provider**, after a driver release contains zwave-js/zwave-js#9396: the minimum driver version check, capabilities, read, allocation on write, clear, release. Breaking Change: Z-Wave locks need that driver release.

PRs 1–3 ship Password on Virtual only, so they can merge before the driver fix. The release goes out with PR 4.

## Open items

- node-zwave-js password encoding: UTF-8 today, the spec requires UTF-16BE (blocks PR 4). HA core's `lock_helpers` length check needs the same fix.
- The sourced Z-Wave User Credential CC dump with password capability (blocks PR 4 tests).
- The follow-up issue for User Code CC alphanumeric locks.

    What the views are told of a slot when the lock gave no PIN for it.

    code. The dashboard cards compare a slot's code against them, and
    ``ts/types.ts`` declares each one as a ``SLOT_CODE_*`` constant.

    EMPTY: the lock says the slot is clear.

    UNREADABLE_CODE: the lock holds a code it will not show (Matter and
    masking locks). Distinct from Home Assistant's STATE_UNKNOWN ("unknown"),
    a sensor whose state is not yet known.

    UNANSWERED: the lock answered without saying anything about the slot. The
    slot may be clear or may hold a code.

    DISABLED: the lock holds a code for the slot that is not in force.

    CHECKING: a managed slot whose last reading was set aside to read it
    again, on a lock that has answered. Nothing is known of it until the read.

    NOT_REPORTED: the lock answered that it cannot tell what the slot holds
    (Zigbee user status Not Supported, #1581).

    EMPTY = "empty"
    UNREADABLE_CODE = "unreadable_code"
    UNANSWERED = "unanswered"
    DISABLED = "disabled_on_lock"
    CHECKING = "checking"
    NOT_REPORTED = "not_reported"


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class SlotCredential:
    """

    Three constructors:
    - ``empty()`` -- slot is cleared on the lock
    - ``unreadable()`` -- slot holds a code whose value is write-only
    - ``known(pin)`` -- slot holds a code whose value the provider exposes

    Treat as opaque; consume via accessors not direct field access.
    """

    present: bool
    pin: str | None

    @classmethod
    def empty(cls) -> SlotCredential:
        """Return the shared "slot is cleared" credential."""
        return _EMPTY_CREDENTIAL

    @classmethod
    def unreadable(cls) -> SlotCredential:
        """Return the shared "slot holds a write-only code" credential."""
        return _UNREADABLE_CREDENTIAL

    @classmethod
    def known(cls, pin: str) -> SlotCredential:
        """Return a credential carrying a readable PIN."""
        return cls(present=True, pin=pin)

    @property
    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        """Return True when the slot holds no code."""
        return not self.present

    @property
    def is_present(self) -> bool:
        """Return True when the slot holds a code."""
        return self.present

    @property
    def is_readable(self) -> bool:
        """Return True when the credential exposes a comparable PIN."""
        return self.present and self.pin is not None

    @property

class CredentialType(StrEnum):
    """
    Kind of credential a user presents to a lock.

    Lock Code Manager writes only ``PIN`` (``MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES``), but
    a use is reported as whichever kind the lock says was presented: ``PIN``,
    ``RFID`` or ``FINGERPRINT`` (Matter, ZHA, Zigbee2MQTT) or ``FACE``
    (Matter). ``PASSWORD`` and ``NFC`` are reserved so a future expansion to
    more kinds is additive. The members map cleanly to both the Z-Wave User
    Credential Command Class and the Matter DoorLock cluster credential-type
    vocabularies. ``PIN`` deliberately serializes to the lowercase wire value
    the providers already send.
    """

    PIN = "pin"
    RFID = "rfid"  # Radio Frequency Identification tag/card.
    FINGERPRINT = "fingerprint"
    FACE = "face"
    PASSWORD = "REDACTED"
    NFC = "nfc"  # Near Field Communication tag.

# write to a lock. Only PIN today, because a slot holds one PIN per user, and
# that is the only credential this integration knows how to produce.
#
# The single place to change when that stops being true. Do not restate the
# set anywhere else: the point of naming it is that "PIN is the only one" is a
# fact about today rather than an invariant, and every site that assumes it
# has to move together.
#
# Distinct from what a lock can REPORT. A lock may advertise types Lock Code
# Manager cannot write -- an RFID reader on the door is one -- and a use of
# one of those is still a use worth recording.

class UserType(StrEnum):
    """
    How a user is constrained on the lock.

    Modeled minimally for now. ``UNRESTRICTED`` matches the Matter and Z-Wave
    "normal" user with no schedule restrictions, which is the only kind Lock
    Code Manager manages today. Additional kinds (for example schedule- or
    duress-restricted users) can be appended without breaking callers.
    """

    UNRESTRICTED = "unrestricted"


class CredentialRule(StrEnum):
    """
    How many credentials a user must present to operate the lock.

    Modeled minimally for now. ``SINGLE`` means one credential is sufficient,
    matching today's one-PIN-per-user reality. Multi-credential rules can be
    appended later without breaking callers.
    """

    SINGLE = "single"

    delegate to that state so there is one source of truth for empty /
    write-only / readable. Treat as an immutable value; consume via the
    accessors rather than reaching into ``state``.
