    type: CredentialType
    slot: int
    state: SlotCredential

    @property
    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        """Return True when the credential's slot holds no code."""
        return self.state.is_empty

    @property
    def is_present(self) -> bool:
        """Return True when the credential's slot holds a code."""
        return self.state.is_present

    @property
    def is_readable(self) -> bool:
        """Return True when the credential exposes a comparable value."""
        return self.state.is_readable

    @property
    def readable_pin(self) -> str | None:
        """Return the value when readable, otherwise ``None``."""
        return self.state.readable_pin

    """
    Stable address for a single credential.

    A lightweight ``(user_id, type, slot)`` tuple used to point at a
    credential without carrying its state. Hashable, so it works as a
    dictionary key or set member when correlating credentials across reads.
    """

    user_id: int
    type: CredentialType
    slot: int

    """
    Address of one credential in Lock Code Manager's own keyspace.

    Distinct from ``CredentialRef``, which addresses a credential on the
    *device* using the identifiers the lock allocated. ``CredentialAddress``
    is the integration-side handle the coordinator and the sync engine key
    on: which managed user, and which kind of credential.

    ``user_ref`` is the managed slot number. An entry owns a slot and every
    credential type in it, so the sync registry (``slot_of``) and the lock
    store key by it.
    """

    user_ref: int
    credential_type: CredentialType

    @override
    def __str__(self) -> str:
        """Name the address in logs: its slot and credential type."""
        return f"{self.user_ref} {self.credential_type}"


def managed_addresses(user_ref: int) -> tuple[CredentialAddress, ...]:
    """Return every credential address Lock Code Manager keeps in sync for a user."""
    return tuple(
        CredentialAddress(user_ref, credential_type)
        for credential_type in sorted(MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES)
    )


def pin_address(user_ref: int) -> CredentialAddress:
    """
    Build the Personal Identification Number address for a managed user.

    Every address in the integration is a PIN address today. This exists so
    the call sites that assume that say so explicitly, and so adding a
    second credential type surfaces each one as a place that needs a
    decision rather than silently continuing to mean PIN.
    """
    return CredentialAddress(user_ref, CredentialType.PIN)


@dataclass(slots=True)
class User:
    """
    A lock user and the credentials they present.

    Modeled so the future "user is the unit, multiple credentials" world is
    additive: today every user carries a single Personal Identification
    Number credential, but ``credentials`` is already a list and the rule and
    type fields already exist. ``credentials`` is mutable (a list), so this
    aggregate is intentionally not frozen; the contained ``Credential``
    values are themselves immutable.
    """

    name: str | None = None
    user_type: UserType = UserType.UNRESTRICTED
    active: bool = True
    credential_rule: CredentialRule = CredentialRule.SINGLE
    credentials: list[Credential] = field(default_factory=list)

    def credentials_of_type(self, credential_type: CredentialType) -> list[Credential]:
        """
        Return this user's credentials of ``credential_type``.

        Generic per-type accessor used by the base orchestration to project
        users into a slot-shaped view for a given credential kind. Providers
        store every type they can map (see each provider's ``async_get_users``);
        this accessor is the seam where the integration narrows that store to
        the type the caller cares about, which today is always Personal
        Identification Number but is wired through here so that adding a
        second supported type (Z-Wave User Credential CC also exposes
        ``PASSWORD``) is a caller-side change, not a provider-side change.
        """
        return [
            credential
            for credential in self.credentials
            if credential.type is credential_type
        ]

    @property
    def pin_credentials(self) -> list[Credential]:
        """
        Return this user's Personal Identification Number credentials.

        Thin alias for ``credentials_of_type(CredentialType.PIN)``; kept as
        a property because most call sites are written against the PIN-only
        world and read cleanly that way.
        """
        return self.credentials_of_type(CredentialType.PIN)


class WriteResult(StrEnum):
    """
    Outcome of a credential write (``async_set_credential``).

    - ``NO_CHANGE`` -- the value was already set; nothing was written.
    - ``CONFIRMED`` -- the write was accepted.
    - ``OPTIMISTIC`` -- the write returned an ambiguous result we treat as
      completed but have NOT confirmed (e.g. a Z-Wave driver
      ``ERROR_UNKNOWN`` from a masked read-back).

    The core does not act on the result (``ha/adapter.py``): the lock's
    worker reads every write back, and the read decides.
    """

    NO_CHANGE = "no_change"
    CONFIRMED = "confirmed"
    OPTIMISTIC = "optimistic"

    @property
    def changed(self) -> bool:
        """Return whether a write actually occurred (CONFIRMED or OPTIMISTIC)."""
        return self is not WriteResult.NO_CHANGE


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class SetUserResult:
    """
    Outcome of creating or updating a lock user.

    ``user_id`` is the resolved identifier, which the integration may allocate
    rather than echo back. ``created`` is True when the call added a new user
    and False when it updated an existing one. The base orchestration uses
    ``created`` to roll back -- delete the user -- only when a newly created
    user would otherwise be left with no credential by a failed credential
    write, preserving the invariant that a user exists if and only if it owns
    at least one credential.
    """

    user_id: int
    created: bool


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class CredentialTypeCapability:
    """
    Per-credential-type limits advertised by a lock.

    ``num_slots`` is the number of slots the lock exposes for this credential
    type, ``min_length`` / ``max_length`` bound an acceptable value, and
    ``supports_learn`` is True when the lock can enroll the credential at the
    device (for example a fingerprint learn flow) rather than being told the
    value.

    Length convention shared by every provider: a non-positive ``max_length``
    means "no advertised maximum / unknown" -- never a literal zero-length
    limit, which would be meaningless -- so providers map an absent or
    unreadable maximum to ``0`` (Matter's ``max_pin_length or 0`` idiom). A
    non-positive ``min_length`` means "no minimum". ``length_bounds`` applies
    this normalization; do not emit a literal ``0`` to express a real limit.
    """

    num_slots: int
    min_length: int
    max_length: int
    supports_learn: bool


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class LockCapabilities:
    """
    What a lock can do, as a platform-neutral snapshot.

    ``supports_user_management`` mirrors the providers' existing gate;
    ``max_users`` is the total number of users the lock can hold; and
    ``credential_types`` maps each supported ``CredentialType`` to its
    per-type limits. A type absent from the mapping is unsupported.
    """

    supports_user_management: bool
    max_users: int
    credential_types: Mapping[CredentialType, CredentialTypeCapability]
    # Maximum user-name length the lock will store; 0 means the lock has
    # no concept of named users (e.g. Z-Wave User Code CC) and the user
    # IS the credential. The base orchestration skips the separate user
    # write when ``supports_user_management`` is False OR this is 0.
    max_user_name_length: int = 0

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        """Snapshot credential_types so the value object cannot be mutated later."""
        object.__setattr__(
            self,
            "credential_types",
            MappingProxyType(dict(self.credential_types)),
        )

    def capability_for(
        self, credential_type: CredentialType
    ) -> CredentialTypeCapability | None:
        """Return the per-type limits for ``credential_type``, else ``None``."""
        return self.credential_types.get(credential_type)

    def supports(self, credential_type: CredentialType) -> bool:
        """Return True when the lock advertises ``credential_type``."""
        return credential_type in self.credential_types

    def bounded_slot_count(self, credential_type: CredentialType) -> int | None:
        """
        Return the slot count to bound against, or ``None`` when unknown.

        ``None`` covers both an unadvertised credential type and a
        ``num_slots`` of 0, which means "capacity unknown" rather than "no
        slots": Matter reports 0 for a capacity field the lock did not
        supply, and a lock that cannot answer must never be treated as
        having nowhere to write. Callers use ``None`` to skip a bounds
        check rather than to reject.

        This lives here so the 0-means-unknown convention is stated once.
        Every caller that re-derived it would be one place for a lock with
        an unreadable capacity to start failing writes it should accept.
        """
        capability = self.capability_for(credential_type)
        if capability is None or capability.num_slots <= 0:
            return None
        return capability.num_slots

    def length_bounds(
        self, credential_type: CredentialType
    ) -> tuple[int, int | None] | None:
        """
        Return the effective ``(min, max)`` value length for a credential type.

        ``None`` when the type is unsupported. A non-positive advertised
        bound means "unbounded" rather than a literal limit: Matter reports
        ``max_pin_length`` as ``... or 0``, where ``0`` is "unknown", so it
        normalizes to no upper bound (``max`` of ``None``). A non-positive
        minimum normalizes to ``0`` (no minimum).
        """
        cap = self.capability_for(credential_type)
        if cap is None:
            return None
        return (
            max(cap.min_length, 0),
            cap.max_length if cap.max_length > 0 else None,
        )


def credential_from_slot(slot: int, state: SlotCredential) -> Credential:
    """
    Build the Personal Identification Number credential for a managed slot.

    The new model relates to the slot-level ``SlotCredential`` by a
    one-to-one projection: a managed slot index becomes a PIN ``Credential``
    at the same index, reusing the ``SlotCredential`` verbatim as its state.
    """
    return Credential(type=CredentialType.PIN, slot=slot, state=state)


def user_from_slot(slot: int, state: SlotCredential, name: str | None = None) -> User:
    """
    Build the single-credential user for a managed slot.

    Realizes today's one-managed-slot to one-user to one-PIN-credential
    projection: the user identifier shares the slot index, the user owns
    exactly one PIN credential at that index, and the user is active exactly
    when the slot holds a code. A future multi-credential world only appends
    to ``credentials`` -- no field changes here.
    """
    return User(
        user_id=slot,
        name=name,
        active=state.is_present,
        credentials=[credential_from_slot(slot, state)],
    )

    # IS the credential. The base orchestration skips the separate user
    # write when ``supports_user_management`` is False OR this is 0.

        """Snapshot credential_types so the value object cannot be mutated later."""
        object.__setattr__(
            self,
            "credential_types",
            MappingProxyType(dict(self.credential_types)),
        )

        self, credential_type: CredentialType
    ) -> CredentialTypeCapability | None:
        """Return the per-type limits for ``credential_type``, else ``None``."""

        """Return True when the lock advertises ``credential_type``."""

    def bounded_slot_count(self, credential_type: CredentialType) -> int | None:
        """

        supply, and a lock that cannot answer must never be treated as
        having nowhere to write. Callers use ``None`` to skip a bounds
        check rather than to reject.

        Every caller that re-derived it would be one place for a lock with
        an unreadable capacity to start failing writes it should accept.
        """
        capability = self.capability_for(credential_type)
        if capability is None or capability.num_slots <= 0:
            return None
        return capability.num_slots

    def length_bounds(
        self, credential_type: CredentialType
    ) -> tuple[int, int | None] | None:
        """
        Return the effective ``(min, max)`` value length for a credential type.

        bound means "unbounded" rather than a literal limit: Matter reports

        normalizes to no upper bound (``max`` of ``None``). A non-positive
        minimum normalizes to ``0`` (no minimum).
        """
        cap = self.capability_for(credential_type)
        if cap is None:
            return None
        return (
            max(cap.min_length, 0),
            cap.max_length if cap.max_length > 0 else None,
        )

    """
    Build the Personal Identification Number credential for a managed slot.

    The new model relates to the slot-level ``SlotCredential`` by a
    one-to-one projection: a managed slot index becomes a PIN ``Credential``
    at the same index, reusing the ``SlotCredential`` verbatim as its state.
    """
    return Credential(type=CredentialType.PIN, slot=slot, state=state)


def user_from_slot(slot: int, state: SlotCredential, name: str | None = None) -> User:
    """
    Build the single-credential user for a managed slot.

    Realizes today's one-managed-slot to one-user to one-PIN-credential
    projection: the user identifier shares the slot index, the user owns
    exactly one PIN credential at that index, and the user is active exactly
    when the slot holds a code. A future multi-credential world only appends
    to ``credentials`` -- no field changes here.
    """
    return User(
        user_id=slot,
        name=name,
        active=state.is_present,
        credentials=[credential_from_slot(slot, state)],

    ``ts/types.ts`` declares each one as a ``SLOT_CODE_*`` constant.

    EMPTY: the lock says the slot is clear.

    masking locks). Distinct from Home Assistant's STATE_UNKNOWN ("unknown"),

    pin: str | None

        return _UNREADABLE_CREDENTIAL

    def known(cls, pin: str) -> SlotCredential:

    """
    Outcome of creating or updating a lock user.

    rather than echo back. ``created`` is True when the call added a new user
    and False when it updated an existing one. The base orchestration uses
    ``created`` to roll back -- delete the user -- only when a newly created
    user would otherwise be left with no credential by a failed credential
    write, preserving the invariant that a user exists if and only if it owns
    at least one credential.
    """

    user_id: int
    created: bool


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class CredentialTypeCapability:
    """
    Per-credential-type limits advertised by a lock.

    ``num_slots`` is the number of slots the lock exposes for this credential
    type, ``min_length`` / ``max_length`` bound an acceptable value, and
    ``supports_learn`` is True when the lock can enroll the credential at the
    device (for example a fingerprint learn flow) rather than being told the
    value.

    Length convention shared by every provider: a non-positive ``max_length``
    means "no advertised maximum / unknown" -- never a literal zero-length
    limit, which would be meaningless -- so providers map an absent or
    unreadable maximum to ``0`` (Matter's ``max_pin_length or 0`` idiom). A
    non-positive ``min_length`` means "no minimum". ``length_bounds`` applies
    this normalization; do not emit a literal ``0`` to express a real limit.
    """

    num_slots: int
    min_length: int
    max_length: int
    supports_learn: bool


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class LockCapabilities:
    """
    What a lock can do, as a platform-neutral snapshot.

    ``supports_user_management`` mirrors the providers' existing gate;
    ``max_users`` is the total number of users the lock can hold; and
    ``credential_types`` maps each supported ``CredentialType`` to its
    per-type limits. A type absent from the mapping is unsupported.
    """

    supports_user_management: bool
    max_users: int
    credential_types: Mapping[CredentialType, CredentialTypeCapability]
    # Maximum user-name length the lock will store; 0 means the lock has
    # no concept of named users (e.g. Z-Wave User Code CC) and the user
    # IS the credential. The base orchestration skips the separate user
    # write when ``supports_user_management`` is False OR this is 0.
    max_user_name_length: int = 0

        """Snapshot credential_types so the value object cannot be mutated later."""
        object.__setattr__(

        self, credential_type: CredentialType
    ) -> CredentialTypeCapability | None:
        """Return the per-type limits for ``credential_type``, else ``None``."""
        return self.credential_types.get(credential_type)

    def supports(self, credential_type: CredentialType) -> bool:
        """Return True when the lock advertises ``credential_type``."""
        return credential_type in self.credential_types

    def bounded_slot_count(self, credential_type: CredentialType) -> int | None:
        """
        Return the slot count to bound against, or ``None`` when unknown.

        ``None`` covers both an unadvertised credential type and a
        ``num_slots`` of 0, which means "capacity unknown" rather than "no
        slots": Matter reports 0 for a capacity field the lock did not
        supply, and a lock that cannot answer must never be treated as
        having nowhere to write. Callers use ``None`` to skip a bounds
        check rather than to reject.

        This lives here so the 0-means-unknown convention is stated once.
        Every caller that re-derived it would be one place for a lock with
        an unreadable capacity to start failing writes it should accept.
        """
        capability = self.capability_for(credential_type)
        if capability is None or capability.num_slots <= 0:
            return None
        return capability.num_slots

    def length_bounds(
        self, credential_type: CredentialType
    ) -> tuple[int, int | None] | None:
        """
        Return the effective ``(min, max)`` value length for a credential type.

        ``None`` when the type is unsupported. A non-positive advertised
        bound means "unbounded" rather than a literal limit: Matter reports
        ``max_pin_length`` as ``... or 0``, where ``0`` is "unknown", so it
        normalizes to no upper bound (``max`` of ``None``). A non-positive
        minimum normalizes to ``0`` (no minimum).
        """
        cap = self.capability_for(credential_type)
        if cap is None:
            return None
        return (
            max(cap.min_length, 0),
            cap.max_length if cap.max_length > 0 else None,
        )


def credential_from_slot(slot: int, state: SlotCredential) -> Credential:
    """
    Build the Personal Identification Number credential for a managed slot.

    The new model relates to the slot-level ``SlotCredential`` by a
    one-to-one projection: a managed slot index becomes a PIN ``Credential``
    at the same index, reusing the ``SlotCredential`` verbatim as its state.
    """
    return Credential(type=CredentialType.PIN, slot=slot, state=state)


def user_from_slot(slot: int, state: SlotCredential, name: str | None = None) -> User:
    """
    Build the single-credential user for a managed slot.

    Realizes today's one-managed-slot to one-user to one-PIN-credential
    projection: the user identifier shares the slot index, the user owns
    exactly one PIN credential at that index, and the user is active exactly
    when the slot holds a code. A future multi-credential world only appends
    to ``credentials`` -- no field changes here.
    """
    return User(
        user_id=slot,
        name=name,
        active=state.is_present,
        credentials=[credential_from_slot(slot, state)],
    )

   461	async def _async_rebuild_if_re_paired(hass: HomeAssistant, lock: str) -> None:
   462	    """
   463	    Start ``lock``'s worker over if its entity id now names another device.
   464

   466	    holder stops the worker; they set up again, building a new provider and
   467	    worker with every slot they want. The old worker stops as a lock leaving
   468	    Lock Code Manager does (``_re_paired``). Clears owed to the old device
   469	    are moot: it is gone; a repair names their slots, which the same lock
   470	    re-paired may still hold.
   471	    """

   473	    registry = lock_registry(hass)
   474	    if (worker := registry.worker(lock)) is None or not _re_paired(hass, lock, worker):
   475	        return  # not running, removed, or the same device (perhaps renamed)

   477	        entry
   478	        for entry in iter_loaded_lcm_entries(hass)
   479	        if lock in entry.runtime_data.locks
   480	    ]
   481	    if not holders:
   482	        return
   483	    _LOGGER.info("%s is a different device now (re-paired): starting it over", lock)

   486	    for address in [a for a, s in worker.slots.items() if s.release]:

   489	        data[GIVEN_UP_KEY].pop((lock, slot), None)

   491	        *(hass.config_entries.async_unload(entry.entry_id) for entry in holders),
   492	        return_exceptions=True,
   493	    )
   494	    for entry, result in zip(holders, unloaded, strict=True):
   495	        if isinstance(result, BaseException):
   496	            _LOGGER.error(
   497	                "Unloading %s for re-paired %s failed: %s", entry.title, lock, result
   498	            )
   499	    if registry.worker(lock) is worker and all(result is True for result in unloaded):
   500	        # Every holder let go, and a one-off read still holds it: the entries
   501	        # take it back, and the lock stays on the old device until they set
   502	        # up again. Not retried when the read is done: nothing says when
   503	        # that is. (A holder not unloaded -- a reload under way -- is not a
   504	        # read: it lets go, and sets up on the new device, on its own.)

   506	            "%s was re-paired, but a read of it was still going: reload Lock "
   507	            "Code Manager to use the new device",

   509	        )

   511	            hass,
   512	            DOMAIN,
   513	            per_lock_issue_id(RE_PAIRED_RELOAD, lock),
   514	            is_fixable=False,
   515	            severity=IssueSeverity.WARNING,
   516	            translation_key=RE_PAIRED_RELOAD,
   517	            translation_placeholders={"lock_entity_id": lock},
   518	        )

   520	        # One set up again meanwhile (a reload), not unloaded, or deleted
   521	        # meanwhile is left be. Setting up raises for nothing else: a failed
   522	        # setup is the entry's state, not an exception.
   523	        if (
   524	            entry.state is not ConfigEntryState.NOT_LOADED
   525	            or hass.config_entries.async_get_entry(entry.entry_id) is not entry
   526	        ):
   527	            continue

   855	    # worker's to resolve: its repair stays until it is tried again.

    67	def lock_error(
    68	    err: LockCodeManagerProviderError, *, clearing: bool
    69	) -> LockError | None:
    70	    """
    71	    Return what a provider's error on a write means to the worker; None for a bug.
    72	
    73	    A refusal is the lock's answer about the slot. Any other failure is no
    74	    answer: providers wrap an integration or cloud outage as a failed
    75	    operation, and a slot is still charged when the lock answers anything
    76	    else in its sync, such as the read-back.
    77	    """
    78	    if isinstance(err, CodeRejectedError):
    79	        # A refused clear holds at once; a refused PIN turns the slot off.
    80	        kind = ErrorKind.SLOT_REFUSED if clearing else ErrorKind.VALUE_REFUSED
    81	    elif isinstance(err, LockOperationUnsupported):
    82	        kind = ErrorKind.SLOT_REFUSED
    83	    elif isinstance(err, (LockOperationError, LockBusy)):
    84	        kind = ErrorKind.NO_ANSWER
    85	    else:
    86	        return None
    87	    cause = str(err) if isinstance(err, LockOperationBlocked) else ""
    88	    return LockError(kind, message=str(err), cause=cause)

    94	    def __init__(
    95	        self,
    96	        provider: BaseLock,
    97	        name_for: Callable[[int], str | None] = lambda slot: None,
    98	        polling: Callable[[], bool] = lambda: True,

   100	        on_reports: Callable[[], None] = lambda: None,
   101	    ) -> None:
   102	        """
   103	        Wrap ``provider``.
   104	
   105	        ``name_for`` names the user a slot's PIN is written for; ``polling``
   106	        says whether the lock is polled ("Disable polling" spares the drift
   107	        check). ``reports`` is shared by every port for the run: lock's
   108	        entity registry id -> whether a read of it has described a slot (see
   109	        ``read``), so a device re-paired under the same entity id starts over;
   110	        ``on_reports`` is called when a read of this lock first does.
   111	        """
   112	        self.provider = provider
   113	        self.name_for = name_for
   114	        self.polling = polling
   115	        # The worker that owns the lock: set once it is built.
   116	        self.worker: LockWorker[CredentialAddress, ProviderPort] | None = None
   117	        # The slot a write is in the provider for: its own echo is not the lock.
   118	        self._writing: int | None = None
   119	        # When each slot was last written, on the event loop's clock: a
   120	        # provider whose reads lag its writes reads it as silent until then.
   121	        self._written_at: dict[int, float] = {}
   122	        # Slots given up: clearing one releases it -- nothing untagged is
   123	        # adopted, and a native-user provider deletes the user it tagged.
   124	        self.releasing: set[int] = set()
   125	        # Of those, the ones the store showed a PIN Lock Code Manager wrote
   126	        # when the release began: the release's own send forgets it.
   127	        self._written: set[int] = set()
   128	        # What the lock last said of any slot, by read or by push: codes
   129	        # nobody here manages, and the last word on a slot the worker has let
   130	        # go. The worker's own view of a slot it tracks comes first.
   131	        self.others: dict[int, Reading] = {}
   132	        # Some read has said something about a slot: silence is now no answer.
   133	        self._answered = False
   134	        # Every lock read this run, by registry id -> whether a read described
   135	        # a slot of it. Kept past this port: a one-off read builds a port per
   136	        # read.
   137	        self.reports: dict[str, bool] = {} if reports is None else reports
   138	        self.on_reports = on_reports
   139	        # Slots the lock last answered it cannot tell what they hold.
   140	        self.not_reported: set[int] = set()
   141	        self._poll: asyncio.Task[None] | None = None
   142	        self._poll_unsubs: list[Callable[[], None]] = []
   143	        # Unloaded: nothing may start a poll or arm its timer again.
   144	        self._closed = False
   145	        # This port set the provider up, and owns its lifecycle.
   146	        self._managed = False
   147	        # Its setup raised what no provider handler expects: nothing retries
   148	        # that short of a reload, so nothing can be sent to the lock.
   149	        self.setup_crashed = False
   150	        self._unsubs: list[Callable[[], None]] = []

   152	    @property
   153	    def managed(self) -> bool:

   159	    async def _timed[T](
   160	        self, op: str, slots: Any, call: Callable[[], Awaitable[T]]
   161	    ) -> T:
   162	        """Run one provider call, logging its start and how long it took."""
   163	        entity_id = self.provider.lock.entity_id
   164	        _LOGGER.debug("%s slot %s: provider %s start", entity_id, slots, op)
   165	        start = time.monotonic()
   166	        outcome = "ok"
   167	        try:
   168	            return await call()
   169	        except BaseException as err:
   170	            kind = getattr(err, "kind", None)
   171	            outcome = kind.value if isinstance(kind, ErrorKind) else type(err).__name__
   172	            raise
   173	        finally:
   174	            _LOGGER.debug(
   175	                "%s slot %s: provider %s %s in %.0f ms",
   176	                entity_id,
   177	                slots,
   178	                op,
   179	                outcome,
   180	                (time.monotonic() - start) * 1000,
   181	            )

   183	    async def read(
   184	        self, addresses: Collection[CredentialAddress]
   185	    ) -> dict[CredentialAddress, Reading]:
   186	        """Ask the lock about ``addresses`` now (see ``_read``), timed for the logs."""
   187	        numbers = [self._pin_slot(address) for address in addresses]
   188	        op = (
   189	            "read (hard refresh)"
   190	            if self.provider.fresh_read_is_hard_refresh
   191	            else "read (get usercodes)"
   192	        )
   193	        where = tuple(numbers)
   194	        readings = await self._timed(
   195	            op, where[0] if len(where) == 1 else where, lambda: self._read(numbers)
   196	        )
   197	        return {pin_address(slot): seen for slot, seen in readings.items()}
   198	
   199	    async def _read(self, slots: Collection[int]) -> dict[int, Reading]:
   200	        """
   201	        Ask the lock about ``slots`` now.
   202	
   203	        Bounded by the provider's own budget for a walk of that many slots.
   204	        A slot the lock said nothing about is left out (silent); a read where
   205	        it said nothing about any of them, from a lock that has answered
   206	        reads before, is no answer -- unless, of some, it answered that it
   207	        cannot tell.
   208	
   209	        A slot it answered it cannot tell of is silent too (#1581), unless a
   210	        read has described some slot of the lock this run: a lock that can
   211	        report its codes and will not report this one holds a code there.
   212	        """
   213	        provider = self.provider
   214	        if self._managed and not await self._set_up():
   215	            raise LockError(
   216	                ErrorKind.NO_ANSWER, sent=False, message="provider not set up"
   217	            )
   218	        await self._available()
   219	        fetch = (
   220	            provider.async_hard_refresh_codes
   221	            if provider.fresh_read_is_hard_refresh
   222	            else provider.async_get_usercodes
   223	        )
   224	        provider.last_silent_slots = provider.last_foreign_slots = frozenset()
   225	        provider.last_cannot_tell_slots = frozenset()
   226	        # A slot past the lock's capacity is never asked about: no answer
   227	        # would come, and the lock would be taken for gone (#1398). Its write
   228	        # is refused unsent, which holds it.
   229	        slots = [slot for slot in slots if await self._within_capacity(slot)]
   230	        if not slots:
   231	            # Nothing was asked: not the lock answering, or a probe of a slot
   232	            # past capacity would end an outage's backoff.
   233	            raise LockError(
   234	                ErrorKind.SLOT_REFUSED, sent=False, message="past the lock's capacity"
   235	            )
   236	        try:
   237	            async with asyncio.timeout(provider._operation_budget(len(slots))):
   238	                codes = await fetch(slots)
   239	        except TimeoutError as err:
   240	            raise LockError(ErrorKind.NO_ANSWER, message="read timed out") from err
   241	        except LockCodeManagerProviderError as err:
   242	            if lock_error(err, clearing=False) is None:
   243	                raise
   244	            # A read that failed said nothing about any slot: no answer.
   245	            raise LockError(ErrorKind.NO_ANSWER, message=str(err)) from err
   246	        silent = provider.last_silent_slots & set(slots)
   247	        cannot_tell = provider.last_cannot_tell_slots & silent
   248	        if self._answered and silent >= set(slots) and not cannot_tell:
   249	            raise LockError(ErrorKind.NO_ANSWER, message="the lock said nothing")
   250	        lock = provider.lock.id
   251	        # Any slot asked about and not silent was described, named in the
   252	        # answer or not: a provider projecting only the slots an entry manages
   253	        # (Z-Wave JS's hard refresh) leaves an empty one it was asked about
   254	        # out, and that is no lock that cannot report.
   255	        if not self.reports.get(lock) and set(slots) - silent:
   256	            self.reports[lock] = True
   257	            self.on_reports()
   258	        if self.reports.setdefault(lock, False):
   259	            silent -= cannot_tell
   260	        self.not_reported.difference_update(slots)
   261	        self.not_reported |= cannot_tell
   262	        # The lock answered, but of a slot written too lately to show it yet:
   263	        # left out (silent), so the write is trusted until a later read.
   264	        silent |= self._lagging(slots)
   265	        # Someone else's code at a slot's index is not the slot's: a slot
   266	        # turned off is clear, and one wanting a PIN writes it, which adopts
   267	        # the user (#1695). It is still a code nobody here manages.
   268	        foreign = provider.last_foreign_slots
   269	        readings = {
   270	            slot: Seen.EMPTY if slot in foreign else reading(codes[slot])
   271	            for slot in slots
   272	            if slot in codes and slot not in silent
   273	        }
   274	        heard = {
   275	            slot: reading(credential)
   276	            for slot, credential in codes.items()
   277	            if slot not in silent
   278	        }
   279	        if provider.per_exchange_budget is None:
   280	            # A provider that reads the whole lock in one call tells of every
   281	            # code on it: one it no longer tells of is gone (deleted at the
   282	            # keypad, say). What it said nothing about stays as it was.
   283	            self.others = {
   284	                **{slot: seen for slot, seen in self.others.items() if slot in silent},
   285	                **heard,
   286	            }
   287	        else:
   288	            # One that walks the slots asked for says nothing of the rest.
   289	            self.others.update(heard)
   290	        self._answered = self._answered or bool(readings)
   291	        return readings

   293	    def _duplicate_of(self, slot: int, pin: str) -> int | None:
   294	        """
   295	        Return another slot ``pin`` is on, or is wanted on; None if none.
   296	
   297	        A tracked slot counts by what it wants (one on its way to another
   298	        PIN, or out, does not); any other slot by what the lock said of it.
   299	        """
   300	        tracked = (
   301	            {}
   302	            if self.worker is None
   303	            else {
   304	                address.user_ref: current
   305	                for address, current in self.worker.slots.items()
   306	                if address.credential_type is CredentialType.PIN
   307	            }
   308	        )
   309	        for other, held in self.others.items():
   310	            if other != slot and other not in tracked and held == Holds(pin):
   311	                return other
   312	        return next(
   313	            (
   314	                other
   315	                for other, current in tracked.items()
   316	                if other != slot and current.want == pin and not current.release
   317	            ),
   318	            None,
   319	        )

   321	    def release(self, slot: int, *, written: bool) -> None:

   325	        ``written``: the store shows a PIN Lock Code Manager wrote there.
   326	        Taken now: the worker forgets what it wrote as it sends the clear.
   327	        """
   328	        self.releasing.add(slot)
   329	        if written:
   330	            self._written.add(slot)
   331	        else:
   332	            self._written.discard(slot)

   424	    async def _set_up(self) -> bool:
   425	        """
   426	        Return whether the provider is set up, asking it first if not.
   427	
   428	        Asking is what retries a deferred setup; a provider with no
   429	        connection check (Z-Wave JS) is asked nowhere else. Reads are gated
   430	        too once this port set the provider up: a lock that answers reads
   431	        while every write is refused unsent would charge each slot's sync
   432	        (the read-back answers) and hold it. A provider this port never set
   433	        up (a one-off read's) is only read.
   434	        """
   435	        provider = self.provider
   436	        if not provider.provider_setup_succeeded:
   437	            with contextlib.suppress(LockCodeManagerError):
   438	                await provider.async_internal_is_reachable()
   439	        return provider.provider_setup_succeeded

   441	    def _lagging(self, slots: Collection[int]) -> set[int]:
   442	        """Return the slots written more lately than the provider's reads catch up."""
   443	        if not (lag := self.provider.read_lag):
   444	            return set()
   445	        now = self.provider.hass.loop.time()
   446	        return {
   447	            slot
   448	            for slot in slots
   449	            if (written := self._written_at.get(slot)) is not None
   450	            and now - written < lag
   451	        }

   457	        For providers that ask for it: Z-Wave queues a dead node's commands
   458	        and delivers them whenever it comes back (#139). No answer, so the
   459	        lock backs off; only the worker's answers decide what is charged.
   460	        """
   461	        provider = self.provider
   462	        if not provider.check_available_before_exchange:
   463	            return
   464	        try:
   465	            available = await provider.async_internal_is_reachable()
   466	        except LockCodeManagerError as err:
   467	            raise LockError(ErrorKind.NO_ANSWER, sent=False, message=str(err)) from err

   469	            raise LockError(
   470	                ErrorKind.NO_ANSWER, sent=False, message="device not available"

   497	    async def async_setup(self, config_entry: ConfigEntry) -> None:
   498	        """Set the provider up with the stand-in coordinator; start the cadence."""
   499	        provider = self.provider
   500	        self._managed = True
   501	        try:
   502	            await provider.async_setup_internal(config_entry, _Coordinator(self))
   503	        except Exception:
   504	            self.setup_crashed = True
   505	            raise
   506	        finally:
   507	            # Even if setup raised: the poll reads the lock, and the
   508	            # connection check is what retries a deferred setup.
   509	            self._arm_poll()
   510	            if interval := provider.connection_check_interval:
   511	                self._unsubs.append(
   512	                    async_track_time_interval(
   513	                        provider.hass,
   514	                        self._check_connection,
   515	                        interval,
   516	                        cancel_on_shutdown=True,
   517	                    )
   518	                )

   520	    async def async_unload(self, remove_permanently: bool) -> None:
   521	        """Stop the cadence and unload the provider."""
   522	        self._closed = True
   523	        for unsub in self._unsubs:
   524	            unsub()
   525	        self._unsubs.clear()
   526	        for unsub in self._poll_unsubs:
   527	            unsub()
   528	        self._poll_unsubs.clear()
   529	        if self._poll is not None:
   530	            self._poll.cancel()
   531	            await asyncio.gather(self._poll, return_exceptions=True)
   532	        await self.provider.async_unload(remove_permanently)

   536	    def pushed(self, slot: int, credential: SlotCredential) -> None:
   537	        """Hand the worker what the lock reported on its own about ``slot``."""
   538	        if self.worker is None or slot == self._writing:
   539	            # A provider echoing the write it is making is not the lock.
   540	            return
   541	        self.not_reported.discard(slot)
   542	        if (address := pin_address(slot)) not in self.worker.slots:
   543	            self.others[slot] = reading(credential)
   544	            return
   545	        self.worker.push(address, reading(credential))
   546	
   547	    def poll(self) -> None:
   548	        """Read every slot the worker tracks, unless a poll is still out."""
   549	        if self.worker is None or not self.worker.started:
   550	            return
   551	        if self._poll is None or self._poll.done():
   552	            self._poll = self.provider.hass.async_create_background_task(
   553	                self._read_tracked(), f"Poll {self.provider.lock.entity_id}"
   554	            )
   555	
   556	    def wants_pin(self, slot: int) -> bool:
   557	        """Return whether ``slot`` should hold a PIN."""
   558	        current = (
   559	            None if self.worker is None else self.worker.slots.get(pin_address(slot))
   560	        )
   561	        return current is not None and current.want is not None
   562	
   563	    async def _read_tracked(self) -> None:
   564	        assert self.worker is not None
   565	        try:
   566	            await self.worker.read()
   567	        except LockError as err:
   568	            # The worker has counted it; nothing else to do.
   569	            _LOGGER.debug("Poll of %s failed: %s", self.provider.lock.entity_id, err)
   570	
   571	    def _cadence(self) -> tuple[timedelta | None, timedelta | None]:
   572	        """
   573	        Return the scan interval (a lock that does not push) and the drift check's.
   574	
   575	        Every read is fresh, so both are plain reads; only the scan gives way
   576	        to "Disable polling".
   577	        """
   578	        provider = self.provider
   579	        scan = None if provider.supports_push else provider.usercode_scan_interval
   580	        return scan, provider.hard_refresh_interval
   581	
   582	    def _arm_poll(self) -> None:
   583	        """(Re)start the poll at the provider's cadence as it stands now."""
   584	        for unsub in self._poll_unsubs:
   585	            unsub()
   586	        self._poll_unsubs.clear()
   587	        if self._closed:
   588	            return
   589	        scan, drift = self._cadence()
   590	        for interval, action in ((scan, self._on_scan), (drift, self._on_poll)):
   591	            if interval:
   592	                self._poll_unsubs.append(
   593	                    async_track_time_interval(
   594	                        self.provider.hass, action, interval, cancel_on_shutdown=True
   595	                    )
   596	                )

    async def async_hard_refresh_codes(
        self, slots: Collection[int] | None = None
    ) -> dict[int, SlotCredential]:
        """
        Re-read from the lock device and return the same shape as async_get_usercodes().

        ``slots`` names the slots whose device state must be re-read; ``None``
        means everything. The returned projection is never narrowed by it:
        a read must still name every managed slot. A provider that reads the
        whole device in one call may ignore ``slots``. One that keeps a cache
        re-reads only ``slots`` and projects the rest from the cache: the
        worker's read-back after a write asks about the one slot written, and
        on a marginal radio link the difference between one command and a
        walk of the lock is the difference between confirming the write and
        never confirming it. One with no cache re-reads every managed slot
        plus ``slots``.
        """
        self._raise_not_implemented(
            "async_hard_refresh_codes",
            "Override this method to re-fetch codes from the lock device.",
        )

    async def async_set_usercode(
        self,
        code_slot: int,
        usercode: str,
        name: str | None = None,
        source: Literal["sync", "direct"] = "direct",
    ) -> WriteResult:
        """
        Set a usercode on a code slot via the User->Credential primitives.

        Projects the slot to a single Personal Identification Number
        credential. Native-user providers run the create-on-first user
        lifecycle via ``_set_credential``; slot-only providers write the
        credential directly, addressing it by slot. Returns the provider's
        ``WriteResult`` (NO_CHANGE / CONFIRMED / OPTIMISTIC).
        """
        state = SlotCredential.known(usercode)
        credential = credential_from_slot(code_slot, state)
        pin = self._require_readable_pin(credential)
        if not self.supports_native_users:
            return await self.async_set_credential(
                code_slot, credential, pin, name=name, source=source
            )
        return await self._set_credential(
            user_from_slot(code_slot, state, name),
            credential,
            pin,
            name=name,
            source=source,
        )

    async def async_clear_usercode(self, code_slot: int) -> bool:
        """
        Clear a usercode on a code slot via the User->Credential primitives.

        Slot-only providers address the credential by slot and delete it
        directly. Native-user providers must target the credential's actual
        owning user, which is not assumed to equal the slot index: a
        credential may have been created on the lock by another controller,
        or the integration may have allocated a user identifier that differs
        from the slot. The owning ``user_id`` is resolved from the lock's
        current users and threaded through the ``CredentialRef`` so the
        provider's delete primitive can address the credential precisely.
        The lock-side user stays put; it is torn down only when the slot
        is removed from LCM config (see ``async_release_managed_slot``).
        Returns True if the value changed, False if it was already cleared
        -- and True when the provider cannot determine whether a change
        occurred. Either way the worker reads the slot back.

        A clear adopts no untagged user (#1518). Adoption belongs to the set
        path, where the write that follows tags the user and corrects a wrong
        guess; a clear is an end state -- a slot turned off or released --
        and nothing follows it to correct anything. The untagged user holding
        a PIN at that index is as likely to be one the homeowner made in the
        vendor's app as ours. The cost: a pre-tag install's PIN in a slot
        that is off stays on the lock until the slot is turned on again and
        the write adopts it. The exception is a lock that keeps no user
        records (a Z-Wave User Code lock): no user there can carry a tag, so
        the slot is the identity.
        """
        if not self.supports_native_users:
            ref = CredentialRef(
                user_id=code_slot, type=CredentialType.PIN, slot=code_slot
            )
            return await self.async_delete_credential(ref)

        # Owner resolution matches by the ``lcm:<slot>:`` tag in user.name,
        # falling back to the slot only on a lock with no user records,
        # where ``credential.slot`` is the LCM slot. Matching
        # by ``credential.slot == code_slot`` alone is unsafe once
        # providers let the lock auto-allocate the credential index -- a
        # tagged user for slot A whose credential lands at index B would
        # be mis-matched when clearing slot B.
        users = await self.async_get_users()
        # Both lookups require the user to actually own a PIN credential
        # at the slot we're clearing. Under the persistent-user-anchor
        # lifecycle a tagged user can exist without a PIN (between
        # writes); resolving such a user as the owner would drive a
        # spurious ``async_delete_credential`` call whose provider-
        # specific return value can incorrectly report changed=True.
        owner_user_id: int | None
        try:
            owner_user_id = next(
                user.user_id
                for user in users
                if self.slot_tag(user) == code_slot
                for credential in user.pin_credentials
                if credential.slot == code_slot
            )
        except StopIteration:
            if await self._supports_user_records():
                return False
            owner_user_id = next(
                (
                    user.user_id

    def _require_readable_pin(self, credential: Credential) -> str:
        """
        Return the credential's readable PIN, or raise ``CodeRejectedError``.

        Called by the seam (``async_set_usercode`` and ``_set_credential``)
        before dispatching to the provider's ``async_set_credential``
        override; the resolved ``pin: str`` is threaded through as a
        positional argument so the provider receives a guaranteed string
        and does not need its own defensive check.

        The seam already builds credentials from a string usercode so
        ``readable_pin`` is non-None by construction along that path -- the
        guard catches future regressions (a credential constructed outside
        the seam, a refactor that loses the invariant) and never the
        normal flow. Providers MUST NOT re-add their own readable-pin
        check; doing so duplicates the contract and re-introduces the
        ``or ""`` silent coercion pattern this helper exists to eliminate.
        """
        pin = credential.readable_pin
        if pin is None:
            raise CodeRejectedError(
                code_slot=credential.slot,
                lock_entity_id=self.lock.entity_id,
                reason="cannot write an unreadable credential",
            )

    @final
    async def _set_credential(
        self,
        user: User,
        credential: Credential,
        pin: str,
        *,
        name: str | None,
        source: Literal["sync", "direct"],
    ) -> WriteResult:
        """
        Run the create-on-first user lifecycle around a credential write.

        Native-user only (the slot adapters call the credential primitive
        directly). Asserts the lock advertises ``credential.type`` and
        replaces ``user.name`` with the LCM-tagged name built via
        ``_build_tagged_user_name(credential.slot, user.name)`` before
        handing the user to the provider, so each provider's
        ``async_set_user`` can write the tagged name verbatim. The tag
        carries the slot binding the find-or-create-by-tag lookup
        recovers on subsequent operations. Rolls back a newly-created
        user when the credential write fails so the lock isn't left
        with a credential-less user the slot-keyed coordinator
        can't reconcile. Returns True if the value changed.

        ``pin`` is the resolved readable PIN that the caller (the seam in
        ``async_set_usercode``) has already validated via
        ``_require_readable_pin``; threading it through avoids a second
        validation pass in the provider.
        """
        await self._assert_credential_type_supported(credential)
        if await self._supports_user_records():
            tagged = await self._build_tagged_user_name(credential.slot, user.name)
            if tagged is None:
                # No stable slot tag fits the lock's max_user_name_length --
                # writing a user without one (or with name=None) would break
                # the find-or-create-by-tag lookup the next operation needs.
                # Fail loudly rather than create an unrecoverable user.
                raise LockOperationFailed(
                    f"Lock {self.lock.entity_id} cannot encode a stable slot "
                    f"tag for slot {credential.slot}; refusing to write a "
                    "credential whose owning user could not be re-identified"

            result = await self.async_set_user(user_for_write)
            credential_user_id = result.user_id
            rollback_user_id = result.user_id if result.created else None

            # lock that has just been presumed wedged, taken while still
            # holding the lock's turn. The user it would delete is found by
            # tag and reused on the next write instead.
            if rollback_user_id is not None:

        ``or ""`` silent coercion pattern this helper exists to eliminate.

    async def _set_credential(

        directly). Asserts the lock advertises ``credential.type`` and
        replaces ``user.name`` with the LCM-tagged name built via
        ``_build_tagged_user_name(credential.slot, user.name)`` before
        handing the user to the provider, so each provider's
        ``async_set_user`` can write the tagged name verbatim. The tag
        carries the slot binding the find-or-create-by-tag lookup
        recovers on subsequent operations. Rolls back a newly-created
        user when the credential write fails so the lock isn't left
        with a credential-less user the slot-keyed coordinator
        can't reconcile. Returns True if the value changed.

        ``async_set_usercode``) has already validated via

    async def async_set_usercode(
        self,
        code_slot: int,
        usercode: str,
        name: str | None = None,
        source: Literal["sync", "direct"] = "direct",
    ) -> WriteResult:
        """
        Set a usercode on a code slot via the User->Credential primitives.

        Projects the slot to a single Personal Identification Number
        credential. Native-user providers run the create-on-first user
        lifecycle via ``_set_credential``; slot-only providers write the
        credential directly, addressing it by slot. Returns the provider's
        ``WriteResult`` (NO_CHANGE / CONFIRMED / OPTIMISTIC).

        credential = credential_from_slot(code_slot, state)
        pin = self._require_readable_pin(credential)

                code_slot, credential, pin, name=name, source=source
            )

            user_from_slot(code_slot, state, name),
            credential,
            pin,
            name=name,
            source=source,

    async def async_clear_usercode(self, code_slot: int) -> bool:
        """
        Clear a usercode on a code slot via the User->Credential primitives.

        Slot-only providers address the credential by slot and delete it
        directly. Native-user providers must target the credential's actual
        owning user, which is not assumed to equal the slot index: a
        credential may have been created on the lock by another controller,
        or the integration may have allocated a user identifier that differs
        from the slot. The owning ``user_id`` is resolved from the lock's
        current users and threaded through the ``CredentialRef`` so the
        provider's delete primitive can address the credential precisely.
        The lock-side user stays put; it is torn down only when the slot
        is removed from LCM config (see ``async_release_managed_slot``).
        Returns True if the value changed, False if it was already cleared
        -- and True when the provider cannot determine whether a change
        occurred. Either way the worker reads the slot back.

        A clear adopts no untagged user (#1518). Adoption belongs to the set
        path, where the write that follows tags the user and corrects a wrong
        guess; a clear is an end state -- a slot turned off or released --
        and nothing follows it to correct anything. The untagged user holding
        a PIN at that index is as likely to be one the homeowner made in the
        vendor's app as ours. The cost: a pre-tag install's PIN in a slot
        that is off stays on the lock until the slot is turned on again and
        the write adopts it. The exception is a lock that keeps no user
        records (a Z-Wave User Code lock): no user there can carry a tag, so
        the slot is the identity.
        """
        if not self.supports_native_users:
            ref = CredentialRef(
                user_id=code_slot, type=CredentialType.PIN, slot=code_slot
            )
            return await self.async_delete_credential(ref)

        # Owner resolution matches by the ``lcm:<slot>:`` tag in user.name,
        # falling back to the slot only on a lock with no user records,
        # where ``credential.slot`` is the LCM slot. Matching
        # by ``credential.slot == code_slot`` alone is unsafe once
        # providers let the lock auto-allocate the credential index -- a
        # tagged user for slot A whose credential lands at index B would
        # be mis-matched when clearing slot B.
        users = await self.async_get_users()
        # Both lookups require the user to actually own a PIN credential
        # at the slot we're clearing. Under the persistent-user-anchor
        # lifecycle a tagged user can exist without a PIN (between
        # writes); resolving such a user as the owner would drive a
        # spurious ``async_delete_credential`` call whose provider-
        # specific return value can incorrectly report changed=True.

            return False

            user_id=owner_user_id, type=CredentialType.PIN, slot=code_slot

        credential_type: CredentialType,

        Every slot in scope is present even when empty: the projection
        starts from ``slots`` -- or ``managed_slots`` when the caller names
        none -- mapped to ``SlotCredential.empty()``

        ``async_get_users``. This preserves the slot-keyed contract the
        lock's worker and the slot entities depend on -- a managed slot

        the empty placeholders are load-bearing. Occupied slots

        everything below it slot-shaped and single-type this round.

        type before passing to the coordinator/entities" (Option A in the
        design discussion). Adding a second supported type means calling
        this helper from a second projection method -- providers store
        every type they can map, so no provider changes are required.

        credential type (Z-Wave User Credential CC also exposes
        ``PASSWORD``), revisit whether the coordinator/entities should

        single projection. The provider-side model is already ready for

        # views. Only a lock with user records can tag a user; on one without

        # so a read asks the lock nothing more.

        directly). Asserts the lock advertises ``credential.type`` and

        ``_build_tagged_user_name(credential.slot, user.name)`` before

        ``async_set_user`` can write the tagged name verbatim. The tag

        recovers on subsequent operations. Rolls back a newly-created
        user when the credential write fails so the lock isn't left
        with a credential-less user the slot-keyed coordinator
        can't reconcile. Returns True if the value changed.

                # writing a user without one (or with name=None) would break

content.thinking:
I'm realizing the virtual store is PIN-only keyed by slot, so to support passwords I'd extend CodeSlotData with an optional "password" field, mirroring the existing pattern, and have the virtual async_set_credential branch on credential.type to pick the right field. For the provider interface, I'm thinking the port's async_set_usercode call builds a PIN credential specifically.

I'm now considering how the port should route reads/writes for both PIN and password types: writes could use a generic async_set_credential_value path, while reads would need a password-specific projection alongside the existing PIN-only async_get_usercodes. The tricky part is avoiding duplicate async_get_users calls when a worker needs both PIN and password for the same slots — ideally one provider call returns both, projecting per type, though the hard-refresh path complicates this since it currently only returns PIN data.

Given how PIN-centered the existing `_read` pipeline is (handling silent slots, cannot_tell, foreign, lagging, etc.), generalizing it to arbitrary credential types is a large undertaking that the spec doesn't fully address. I'm leaning toward keeping `_read` as the PIN-only path and adding a separate, simpler `_read_type` path for passwords that skips those side-channel concerns for now, deferring full generalization (including hard-refresh handling) to the Z-Wave PR — a YAGNI-friendly approach that targets Virtual first.

Still, I want at least one consistency rule across types: a managed slot missing from the map should always mean "silent." But stepping back, I'm worried PR 2 itself is too large — covering entities, config, services, validator, coordinator rules, the adapter, and runtime carryover — so I'm considering splitting it into a 2a/2b sequence, though that raises complications like how MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES interacts with per-lock address generation for Virtual locks if password support is added prematurely.

Checking which providers actually expose PASSWORD in their capabilities — Virtual would be affected, Z-Wave's current reporting is uncertain and seems tied to a later PR, and Matter doesn't support it at all — so a 2a split focused on runtime keeping every type a lock supports would mostly only change Virtual's behavior while carrying forward the existing per-slot release, issue, and disable logic from pieces 1-9.

A second PR, 2b, would cover everything password-specific in config and services: validators, subentry fields, YAML support, the credential-required rule, repair renaming, text splitting, labels, sensors, duplicate handling, masking, the generator, and services. Since this reshapes the spec's four-PR plan into five, I think this is really a scope decision for the user to weigh in on, though I can still draft a recommendation and get started on the 2a plan while flagging the change in PR count.

Before surfacing that, I want to be more confident about the full picture — I should look into how the slot coordinator handles wants flowing from config into runtime state, along with entity.py's pin logic and the binary sensor, so let me dig into slot_coordinator next.

I'm realizing the virtual store is PIN-only keyed by slot, so to support passwords I'd extend CodeSlotData with an optional "password" field, mirroring the existing pattern, and have the virtual async_set_credential branch on credential.type to pick the right field. For the provider interface, I'm thinking the port's async_set_usercode call builds a PIN credential specifically.

I'm now considering how the port should route reads/writes for both PIN and password types: writes could use a generic async_set_credential_value path, while reads would need a password-specific projection alongside the existing PIN-only async_get_usercodes. The tricky part is avoiding duplicate async_get_users calls when a worker needs both PIN and password for the same slots — ideally one provider call returns both, projecting per type, though the hard-refresh path complicates this since it currently only returns PIN data.

Given how PIN-centered the existing `_read` pipeline is (handling silent slots, cannot_tell, foreign, lagging, etc.), generalizing it to arbitrary credential types is a large undertaking that the spec doesn't fully address. I'm leaning toward keeping `_read` as the PIN-only path and adding a separate, simpler `_read_type` path for passwords that skips those side-channel concerns for now, deferring full generalization (including hard-refresh handling) to the Z-Wave PR — a YAGNI-friendly approach that targets Virtual first.

Still, I want at least one consistency rule across types: a managed slot missing from the map should always mean "silent." But stepping back, I'm worried PR 2 itself is too large — covering entities, config, services, validator, coordinator rules, the adapter, and runtime carryover — so I'm considering splitting it into a 2a/2b sequence, though that raises complications like how MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES interacts with per-lock address generation for Virtual locks if password support is added prematurely.

Checking which providers actually expose PASSWORD in their capabilities — Virtual would be affected, Z-Wave's current reporting is uncertain and seems tied to a later PR, and Matter doesn't support it at all — so a 2a split focused on runtime keeping every type a lock supports would mostly only change Virtual's behavior while carrying forward the existing per-slot release, issue, and disable logic from pieces 1-9.

A second PR, 2b, would cover everything password-specific in config and services: validators, subentry fields, YAML support, the credential-required rule, repair renaming, text splitting, labels, sensors, duplicate handling, masking, the generator, and services. Since this reshapes the spec's four-PR plan into five, I think this is really a scope decision for the user to weigh in on, though I can still draft a recommendation and get started on the 2a plan while flagging the change in PR count.

Before surfacing that, I want to be more confident about the full picture — I should look into how the slot coordinator handles wants flowing from config into runtime state, along with entity.py's pin logic and the binary sensor, so let me dig into slot_coordinator next.

I'm thinking through release semantics for the registry's give_up flow, making sure each slot's release happens exactly once by routing writes through a provider's managed-slot release call, and designing a tracked set of released slot numbers so a later duplicate release is idempotent and simply returns false, letting a read-back confirm the slot is empty.

Better to prune `_released` inside `release()` itself — discard the slot from `_released` whenever a new release cycle starts, so repeated releases reset properly. Then I realize the base `async_release_managed_slot` only clears the PIN, not other credential types like password — the spec says release should clear every credential type LCM wrote, so the base implementation needs to loop over all managed types the lock supports and clear each one.

I should check which providers currently override these methods before committing to this approach.

def _slot_coordinator_for(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    name: str,
    config_entry_id: str | None,
    config_entry_title: str | None,
) -> SlotEntityCoordinator:
    """Return the coordinator for the slot the named user occupies."""
    config_entry = get_loaded_config_entry(hass, config_entry_id, config_entry_title)
    config = get_entry_config(config_entry)
    stored = _stored_user(config, name)

    # One condition for two ways to hold nothing: a user with no number was
    # never placed, and a number with no coordinator is an entry whose slots
    # and configuration disagree. Both mean there is no slot here to write to
    # or clear, and neither is worth telling apart in the message.
    slot_num = config.assignment.slot(stored)
    coordinators = config_entry.runtime_data.slot_coordinators
    if slot_num is None or (coordinator := coordinators.get(slot_num)) is None:
        raise ServiceValidationError(f"{stored!r} holds no slot in this config entry")
    return coordinator


def _managed_credential_type(credential_type: str) -> CredentialType:
    """
    Return the credential type, refusing kinds this integration cannot write.

    Every member of ``CredentialType`` is accepted by the schema so the
    vocabulary is the providers' rather than this action's, and the ones Lock
    Code Manager cannot yet store are refused here instead -- the caller
    learns that RFID is a real kind that is not supported yet, rather than
    that the word is invalid.
    """
    kind = CredentialType(credential_type)
    if kind not in MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES:
        supported = ", ".join(sorted(MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES))
        raise ServiceValidationError(
            f"Lock Code Manager cannot store a {kind} credential. "
            f"Supported: {supported}"
        )
    return kind


async def async_set_credential(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    name: str,
    *,
    credential_type: str,
    value: str,
    enable_if_disabled: bool = False,
    config_entry_id: str | None = None,
    config_entry_title: str | None = None,
) -> None:
    """
    Set one of a user's credentials, and let the sync carry it to the locks.

    Addresses the user rather than a lock and a slot number. What that buys
    over ``set_usercode`` is that the credential ends up in the
    configuration: a code written straight to a device is one Lock Code
    Manager does not know about, which the sync may clear back out, and which
    cannot reach a member holding its credentials here rather than on a
    device.

    Routed through the slot's coordinator rather than written to the entry,
    because that is the authoritative gate for a credential write -- it strips
    whitespace and validates the length against every bound lock. Writing the
    configuration directly here would be a second path that skips both.

    ``enable_if_disabled`` turns the user on afterwards, which is what makes this the
    inverse of :func:`async_clear_credential` rather than half of it: clearing
    a credential disables the user, so setting one on somebody cleared earlier
    would otherwise leave a code that is present and inert. Off by default,
    because giving a user a credential and letting them in are different
    decisions and only the caller knows whether they are making both.

    Not a field written alongside the PIN: enabling has its own rules -- it
    refuses a user with no credential and clears the repair issue raised when
    that happened -- and the second call is what runs them.
    """
    # Not checked for emptiness here: the schema strips and requires at least
    # one character, so an empty value never reaches this. Repeating that gate
    # would be a branch nothing can take.
    _managed_credential_type(credential_type)
    coordinator = _slot_coordinator_for(hass, name, config_entry_id, config_entry_title)
    await coordinator.async_request_pin_update(value)
    if enable_if_disabled:
        # Safe in this order, and only in this order: the write above refreshes
        # the entry's cached config before returning, so the PIN this checks
        # for is the one just set.
        await coordinator.async_request_active_toggle(True)

content.thinking:
I'm working out how the code sensor should keep using the PIN value while the binary sensor aggregates across multiple addresses, giving each lock worker a default address tuple and figuring out how to determine aggregate status when some addresses might be missing.

The trickier part is making addresses dynamic rather than static, since capabilities can refresh after entity creation — computing the aggregate as "every address this slot currently tracks on the worker" avoids baking in a stale list, but per-type sensors still need the lock's supported credential types known at entity-add time, which raises timing questions about when capabilities get probed versus when entities get created.

Actually, capabilities aren't known at hold time since holding happens before provider setup — so per-lock addresses need to be decided after setup instead. The approach: hold PIN addresses initially, then once capabilities are known, run a refresh step that claims addresses for newly-supported types and releases ones for unsupported types, while being careful that wanting a non-PIN type on a lock that doesn't support it shouldn't cause issues.

Writing to an unsupported type on Z-Wave/Matter would raise an unsupported error and trigger a repair, while reading would just return empty and sync as IN_SYNC — but that still triggers an extra costly read per poll cycle for something like a password type on a Z-Wave lock, since usercodes get fetched as a whole group. So I need capability awareness to avoid adding password addresses to locks that don't support them at all, perhaps by filtering at the port level.

But if I synthesize empty reads for unsupported types without querying the lock, that works for read-only sync but breaks when a write attempt specifies a real value — that write should never happen for unsupported capabilities. So the correct model really needs per-lock address sets built from capabilities, which only become available after provider setup runs in the registry's prepare flow following hold. I want to trace through how registry.hold and prepare work to find where to inject that.

    async def _setup_one_lock(lock_entity_id: str) -> BaseLock | None:
        # Every slot's want goes in with the hold: a new worker reads them all
        # in its first exchange.
        wants = {
            slot_num: coordinator.want
            for slot_num, coordinator in runtime_data.slot_coordinators.items()
        }
        # Holding waits on the lock's provider setup, which has the operation
        # deadline to answer; said long before that.
        still_waiting = hass.loop.call_later(

            _LOGGER.warning,

            # Transport failures degrade inside async_setup_internal, and
            # structural validation failures are logged there and kept
            # degraded, so a popped lock is either a genuine bug or a lock

            # an mqtt device re-discovered under an unrecognized bridge. The
            # config flow refuses that selection, so it cannot arrive here
            # from the selection path.
            _LOGGER.error(
                "%s (%s): Failed to set up lock %s: %s",

                entry_title,
                lock_entity_id,

            )
            if isinstance(err, UnclaimedLockError):
                # Only this failure has a diagnosis and an action to offer.
                # Any other exception is a bug in a provider LCM does speak,
                # and a repair telling that user their bridge is unsupported
                # sends them to remove a lock that works.
                _async_report_dropped_lock(hass, lock_entity_id, err)
            return None
        finally:

        runtime_data.locks[lock_entity_id] = lock

content.thinking:
Since entities get added after provider setup, capabilities should typically already be cached by then, so per-type sensors can rely on cached capabilities at creation time. I'm sketching the "wants per type" API at the HA layer, where the coordinator supplies a mapping of credential type to Want objects for the hold lock function.

The per-lock address resolution needs to intersect managed types with cached capability types, but caps may be unknown at hold time -- so I'm considering a hook that runs after setup to fill in missing types once capabilities are known. The idea is that pushing a want recomputes the per-lock address set from cached caps each time, so after setup completes, any subsequent want push automatically covers newly discovered types, while the initial hold only guarantees the PIN floor if caps are unresolved.

I also need to account for the case where provider setup fails or is deferred during hold, leaving capabilities unknown and PIN-only addresses in play -- once the deferred setup later succeeds and capabilities become known, the want set needs to be recomputed to include the newly available types.

So I'm thinking the port should trigger a callback when setup transitions from failed/unset to succeeded, which would cause the coordinator to re-push wants for that lock across all holder entries. Then async_want recomputes addresses from the freshly cached capabilities each time it's called, so a successful recompute naturally picks up any new credential types.

For types that dropped out of a lock's capabilities, I'm leaning toward calling a forget on the worker rather than a release, so the lock state itself stays untouched while stale type tracking gets cleared. This is a sizable change to async_hold_lock's wants parameter, shifting it to a per-type mapping, but for the minimal viable slice, Virtual is the only lock advertising password and its capabilities are static after setup, so testing an actual mid-flight capability change would need a fake provider rig rather than relying on Virtual.

I want to check whether the base class already has a mechanism for refreshing or resetting cached_capabilities, perhaps tied into a re-interview event, so the capability-refresh trigger isn't something I need to invent from scratch.

async def async_read_occupancy(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    config_entry: ConfigEntry | None,
    locks: Sequence[str],
    indices: Collection[int],
    *,
    progress: Callable[[float], None] | None = None,
) -> Occupancy:
    """
    Ask every lock in ``locks`` which of ``indices`` it holds.

    A lock that cannot answer reports ``None``, never an empty set: that
    difference is what makes allocation refuse instead of issuing a
    number over a credential it never checked for. Every way of failing
    to answer has to arrive that way, including the ones no provider
    promised.

    ``config_entry`` is the entry being allocated for, which is also the
    one entry whose numbers do not constrain the answer: kept ones are held
    by tenure, released ones are free for whoever comes next. ``None`` is
    an entry still being created, which by the same rule holds nothing and
    so excludes nothing.

    ``progress`` is told, as a fraction, how many of the locks have answered,
    as each one does: a lock that answers one index per round trip can take a
    minute or more, and the flow showing this read should not look frozen
    while it waits. The answer keeps the order of ``locks`` however the reads
    finished, so an unreadable set is always named the same way.
    """
    dev_reg = dr.async_get(hass)
    ent_reg = er.async_get(hass)

    async def _read(lock_entity_id: str) -> LockOccupancy:
        try:
            lock_instance = build_lock_instance(
                hass, dev_reg, ent_reg, config_entry, lock_entity_id
            )
        except LockQuerySkipped as skipped:
            return LockOccupancy(
                lock_entity_id=lock_entity_id, managed=skipped.managed, occupied=None
            )

through one provider instance. This machine sets up three entries over two
